In the picturesque world of paragliding, hidden secrets tumble as Detective Winston investigates the brutal hatchet murder of Travis, with only Bryan and Everett in the center of the storm.

Rubbing the backside of his eyes, Winston slowly navigated the case photos scattered across his desk. A paragliding site, bloody and as wide open as the sea, was the setting for Travis's murder. Bryan, known more for his cooking than as a suspect, stepped into the limelight of Winston's investigation. 

It did not go unnoticed that Bryan would carry a hatchet on him for his job; the tool in hand was a common sight that everyone had become accustomed to. Par for the course, it was largely ignored when Bryan was seen sharpening his utensil before the incident; a hatchet taught to kiss the air during Bryan's past hatchet throwing competitions. 

Travis was a known occurence on the local gliding scene. Bryan was his assistant, charged with food and drinks, presumably there to manage as the paragliders soared high above.

"So, you're always left to care for the gliders' needs during the flights, huh?" Winston asked, making sure to keep his tone casual as they approached Bryan, who was preparing a meal.

"Yeah, been doing it for a while now. Help 'em grab a bite at the end of their flight, you know?" Bryan mentioned, chopping some tough ingredients with his hatchet. From his posture and technique, it was clear he knew his way around such a tool.

"The same way you've been helping yourself to the petty cash, I see," Winston casually remarked, causing Bryan to stumble a bit, resulting in him nicking his finger slightly.

"No, that's not..." Bryan lapsed before continuing, his hands trembling. He seemed to be genuinely frightened of the possibility of going to jail.

"Travis didn't seem to think so," Winston subtly pointed out, before changing the topic. "How'd you feel about his pranks?"

Bryan's grip on his hatchet tightened, "He's... been a real handful. Those weren’t just pranks, he's been doing everything in his power to make a fool out of me."

"I suppose you were near the gliding site before the incident happened?" Bryan nodded, confirming that he indeed was, "Yeah, I was there prepping up the food and drinks we're serving today."

In the pink-tinged evening light, Winston walked back from the crime scene towards his car. Whispers of unfriendly pranks, public humiliation, and petty thefts filled the air. Across his mind slipped an image of Travis, alone, soaring in the air.

Detective Winston sat back in his chair, brows furrowed as he perused the pile of evidence on the sturdy wooden table. He meticulously studied the hapless victim - Travis, a man recently celebrated for his acrobatic skills on a paraglider, a man whose life was cut short at a paragliding site with a hatchet.

His suspect was intriguing, to say the least. Everett he was known as, a bright-faced man whose talent lay in the realm of woodworking methods. Interestingly, a majority of his time was dedicated to curating displays of impeccable craftsmanship at the local woodworking museum.

Upon arriving at the museum, Winston took a mental note of the serene aura surrounding Everett. His hands, worn from years of delicate crafting, fondly caressed the various tools in his personal collection. Quiet admiration sparked in his eyes as he studied each piece. The hatchet, which was the murder weapon, had been sourced from this same collection.

Everett had a dubious past, considering he had been privy to the office that housed a drawer filled with FFID cards, each bearing a different alias. The coincidental catalog of names was a matching list to Everett's known aliases.

In a room full of bustling conference attendees, Fraser, a local woodworker, casually recollected an incident about an 'Edward' who introduced himself during a conversation at a conference. This character sketch fit Everett impeccably. Yet another time, Winston learned, Everett introduced himself as 'Eric' within a gathering of familiar faces.

His evenly-toned voice was lit with envy as he recalled the numerous paragliding events where he would always find himself under the grand shadow of the deceased Travis. This bitterness was further accentuated by a recent event where Travis triumphed over Everett for a highly acclaimed paragliding award.

"Do you do much woodworking yourself?" Winston asked.

Everett's eyes softened, his hands gripped tighter around the intricate carving in his hand. "Yes, indeed," he replied. "It's the one thing that brings me peace..."

Parallel to the photo of Travis, paragliding expert propelled to international fame, an unsigned artisan found solace in chipping away at blocks of wood, longing for the same acclaim.

In the grim spectacle of the wrestling ring stained with blood, Detective Winston embarks on a chilling manhunt for Serenity's chainsaw-wielding murderer, revolving around two main suspects: Terrance and Nelson.

Winston mused over his coffee cup, squinting at his notes from last night's wrestling match. Serenity, the star wrestler, had publicly threatened her opponent, Terrance. And Terrance, poor lad, was found pale and trembling after their match. Terrance was no stranger to the grit and physicality of ranch life, but the wrestling ring was another story entirely. He had been in the losing end of a previous matchup with Serenity. 

Finally placated by the caffeine and recalling his purpose, Winston trudged to the boots and scruff leather of the local ranch. He was greeted by the sight of Terrance coordinating his ranch work, his sun-worn skin a testament to long hours under the warm Texan sun. "You're Terrance I suppose?" Winston asked, as he gestured to the flourishing land around them.

"That'd be me, Detective," Terrance replied in a thick southern drawl. "This land's been around longer than I have. Been a rancher all my life."

There was an odd sense of hitched anxiety when Winston brought up the chainsaw classes he'd heard Terrance attended. "Gotta know how to operatin' it," Terrance replied. "Helps keepin' the place run smooth."

Winston hustled over to where the recent wrestling match had taken place. It was a local tradition in the town and Terrance was no stranger to it, being a regular sponsor. It was a sweltering evening when he found himself at the scene, their wrestling ring splattered with the remnants of what occurred.

Returning to the station under the glow of disjointed neon lights, Winston on a hunch asked a few local attendees about the particular wrestling match where Serenity was killed. Terrance was in the crowd that night, cheering heatedly during the match.

In a more relaxed visit to the local bar, Terrance appeared more forthright. "She was strong, Detective. Really strong," Terrance eased into his confession after a few sips of his drink. At another instance, in a low murmured admission to some friends, Terrance had been heard saying he felt threatened by Serenity. There were rumors around of Terrance being seen frequently repairing a chainsaw. The very same chainsaw Terrance learned to operate, and the chilling instrument that ended Serenity's life.

For now, this was the puzzle Winston had to unravel. He gave Terrance a long, discerning look over the rim of his beer glass before leaving the lightly crowded bar. On his way out, the words of a recent reports echoed in his head, “A chainsaw is essential in ranch work…”

Winston had been downing cups of coffee all day, trying to make sense of the pieces of what seemed like a nonsensical puzzle. He made a decision to visit the place it all transpired – an old, grimy wrestling ring where Serenity had met her horrific end.

The image of the chainsaw used as the murder weapon kept coming back to him. So brutal was it that Winston found it hard to shake off. He had heard that Nelson, the painter and prime suspect in the case, had been seen training with a chainsaw - a tool that he directly employed in his painting procedures, forming part of his job. The oddity seemed to strengthen the potential motive Nelson had for this grim act and Winston felt compelled to pursue this lead.

After a quick tour to the local gallery, Winston visited an exhibition where Nelson's pieces were showcased. It was evident that his chainsaw artwork had amassed some level of local attention, owing to their exceptional detailing accomplished with a chainsaw. Nelson adored wood, especially intricate shapes created out of it. He would often proclaim that shaping wood using his chainsaw was an integral part of his painting role. His proficiency seemed uncanny, almost eerie, but the public admired his work for its notable woodsiness.

From the gallery, Winston travelled to the correction facility where Nelson used to work. The officers seemed reluctant to speak about the past events which led to Nelson's termination and the painter's complete obliteration from the collective memory. Winston found no records of Nelson in the personnel files. His data seemed to have been deliberately wiped out, prompting Winston to question their collective avoidance in discussing Nelson.

Winston then moved to his final stop, Nelson's quaint bungalow. Unusually quiet and still with the curtains tightly drawn; not the usual sight, as reported by neighbors who mentioned Nelson's affection for painting under natural light. Winston learned that Nelson had ceased attending the weekly game nights at the local pub, coinciding with his new preference for drawn curtains.

As Winston introspected leaning against his car, he realized the significance of the patterns in the changing behaviors of the painter. Winston was now confident that Nelson indeed had a strong motive in Serenity's demise – albeit, this was supported by an eerie amalgamation of evidence: the drawn curtains, the nonattendance at the pub, the wiped data, the unusual termination, and finally, his habitual, ominous use of chainsaws. 

Time was ticking away, and Winston was now more determined than ever. He drove away from Nelson’s bungalow, deep in thoughts about the painter and his last works that haunted his thoughts. The presentiment of the forthcoming day, the hunt for more truths and the justice for Serenity, was overwhelming. Each passing hour made the air heavier with unspoken truths, and Winston was resolute to unthread them all.

In the daunting terrain of a mountain climbing site, Floyd meets his untimely demise through the barrel of a shotgun, leaving Detective Winston with a chilling whodunit mystery on his hands with prime suspects being Francis and Camille.

Detective Winston peered at the newspaper clipping, the headline "Local Man Hits Lottery Jackpot!" blazoned across the top in bold type. The winning grin of Floyd looking up at him from the grainy print. Alongside the article was another news item where Floyd publicly announced that he was preparing to climb the local mountain solo. Floyd loved mountain climbing. He always found solitude in the mountains - they gave him a sense of tranquility, something he seemed to have desired mathematically and announced vociferously, proclaiming his affection for solo treks. 

Taking a gulp of his black coffee, Winston shifted his gaze to another printout - Floyd's invitation list to his pre-mountaineering celebration and the subsequent solo climbing event at the mountain site. Francis' name was there, highlighted in a fluorescent green marker and was flagged for the mountain site visit. 

Francis, a dedicated potter by trade. The artist held his craft close to his heart, even going so far as painstakingly using a specialized kiln for the inclusion of local insect fauna in his intricate pottery works. A kiln designed in a way to safely house the insects during the firing process, preserving their delicate structures within the hardened clay.

Winston grabbed his hat and coat, his next destination was Francis' pottery shop. The craftsman's shop was filled with interesting pieces - bowls, vases, statues, lots teeming with countless insects immortalized in clay. 

"Detective Winston," Francis greeted, wiping clay off his hands with a stained rag.

"Francis," Winston acknowledged, watching as Francis flitted nervously around his workshop, tidying up the pottery equipment. "I heard you craft some interesting pottery with insects."

"That's right. Gather them myself from the nearby mangroves. Interesting stuff out there. Unique clay too." A glimmer of passion flared in his eyes. 

"Did Floyd ever purchase anything from your shop?" Winston asked, casually, moving to inspect the insect filled vessels.

"He...uh, he confided he wasn't aware of my situation," Francis responded, a slight wistfulness creeping into his voice. "Business has been tough. I borrowed from some less... reputable sources, a loan shark. But with the low sales of my pottery, paying back has been difficult."

Leave it to Winston to know what 'reputable sources' entailed. The phrase 'loan shark' echoed loudly in his mind. 

"I see. Were you aware of Floyd's recent windfall?"

Francis' face turned a shade paler. "Yes, I saw about it in the newspaper."

Winston nodded, plucking a small clay insect from the shelf. 

"Maybe you should spend some time away from this shop, Francis. Take a break, maybe even visit the mangroves or go to the mountain site with Floyd? Could do you some good."

Francis gulped, nodding as he watched Winston make his way out of the store.

The crunch of gravel under Winston's shoes echoed through the night as he left the crime scene and headed toward his next destination. It hadn't been an ordinary Tuesday at all; what with finding Floyd's body on a mountain climbing site, his life ended abruptly by a shotgun blast. On top of everything else, he had just spoken to Floyd's attorney who informed him that Floyd had plans to alter his will.

Winston arrived at his destination - Camille's residence. A quick glance at a recent receipt from a gun shop on the flashy car dashboard beside a valid shotgun permit and the credit card statement visible through the glass, hinted at the daughter’s extravagant spending habits.

Upon entering the living area, Winston noticed papers scattered around. As he examined the documents, he confirmed they were the updated will paperwork the attorney had mentioned - the same ones found in Floyd's study. "Interesting reading material you have there," he commented casually.

Understanding that it was unusual to casually visit a murder suspect’s house during late hours, Winston wet ahead. The door opened to reveal Camille who invited him in.

Camille responded with a brief toss of her head, "Oh, just going through some of Dad's papers. You wouldn't believe the number of documents the man kept."

Winston gave a slight nod and steered the conversation towards mountain climbing. "Dad loved it, invited me numerous times," she confessed.

"And did you accept his invite this last time, Camille?" Winston asked cursorily.

"Yes, I did. In fact, we were the only ones on the mountain. I was on the summit before they found dad" Camille looked away out towards the window.

Detective Winston, careful to maintain neutrality, moved on - shifting his attention towards the pile of papers on Camille's coffee table. As he picked them up, his eyes immediately fell on one - a loan document in Camille's name. "You seem to have quite a collection here," he commented, keeping his tone light.

"I do have a lot of expenses, Detective." Camille defended. She quickly regained her composure and mentioned her recent firearm activities. "I even took shooting classes last summer, you know, just for something different. I even got myself a valid shotgun permit. Oh, and they had an offer on shotguns, so I bought one."

"Shotguns, eh? Do you frequent any local shooting range for practice?" Winston questioned, smooth and casual.

"I did have a couple of sessions at the local one after the classes," Camille admitted, moving around the room, her gaze absent. "According to the range officer, I was a natural with a shotgun."

Winston nodded, admiring her candidness. "Well Camille, I appreciate your time," he finally said, rising from the plush couch, his mind spinning with the connecting pieces of the puzzle. With scant evidence laying on the coffee table and considerable clues hidden in their conversation, it was clear that this case was only beginning.

Background files from related investigations (some may be irrelevant):

In the hushed silence of the library, Floyd lay dead with a shiv protruding from his chest, prompting Detective Winston to weave through the labyrinth of books and suspicion, targeting his primary suspects, Zara and Catherine.

Winston glanced over the crime scene again, the quiet library now a place of death and horror. The victim, Floyd, lay lifeless on the floor, an unlikely end to his ruthless pursuit of money. Floyd had refused to give up on collecting from Catherine, an airline pilot who had fallen on some hard times with missed mortgage payment after missed mortgage payment.

Stepping away from the crime scene, Winston called in a visit to Catherine. Her house felt quiet, almost sparse, a faint memory of better times perhaps reflected in something he noticed frequently in the past few weeks - her obsessively reading through her scrapbook, scanning, examining, dwelling in her past. It was hard to imagine a woman like Catherine having to sell her own plane, but interestingly enough, substantial debt and strain could cause people to do things they wouldn't ordinarily consider.

As Winston noticed Catherine walking up to the front door, an odd sight caught his eye. Catherine was holding her well-thumbed scrapbook in one hand, and newspaper clippings and obituaries littered the ground around her. A more careful look revealed an extensive collection of obituaries forming a large part of her scrapbook. The other hand held a familiar object – a pair of scissors – as she cut out pieces of articles to add to her collection. And discarded scrap clippings ferried by the breeze were scattered about. It was clear that the scrapbook activity was a frequent one. Task completed, she then tucked the scissors back into a bag that also concealed a shiv. Catherine felt a certain sense of comfort and preparedness when she had her shiv at hand. Her military background had made her adept at it, and she had never stopped carrying one, even after leaving the service.

"Catherine?" Winston asked, subtly studying her.

"Yes, that's me," Catherine responded without trying to read into his intent.

"You were in the military, right?"

"Correct. Piloting planes wasn't my start." She retorted, the scars of battles both physical and mental marked meditatively on her persona. Indeed, she was an unlikely debtor, having once been highly trained personnel in military combat – the shiv was her preferred weapon, which she'd practiced with consistently after her service days.

Winston noticed the agitation in her eyes as they turned to the topic of Floyd. It was evident Floyd's continuous demand for money had stirred up enough frustration and desperation within Catherine, and the fact that he was planning to take legal action against her only added fuel to the fire.

"Well, Catherine. Nice talking to you," Winston said, standing up from the porch steps. "This is routine, we're talking to everyone Floyd knew."

"Of course, detective. I understand," Catherine said, her rigid military bearing showing through.

As Winston drove away, he couldn't help but replay the entire conversation in his head. Flight or fight. In Catherine’s case, she was always prepared to do either, hence the shiv in her bag. With her financial situation forcing her into a corner, it seemed like fight was becoming her only option.

Winston browsed through the case file while sipping his freshly brewed coffee. The victim, Floyd, was found dead in the library, dead from puncture and cut wounds, potentially from a shiv- an easy enough weapon to make or find.

He sat back in his chair, looking over the CCTV footage from the library. The video stream showed Zara, a local fashion designer known for her extravagant style and equally extravagant temper, walking in and out of the library on the day of the crime. That wouldn't normally place her as a suspect... if it hadn't been for the fact that Floyd and Zara didn't exactly get along.

Floyd had told friends on numerous occasions how Zara had asked him for money, a request he'd always refused. Winston flicked through more notes - Zara had been spending a frightening amount of money on drugs, and her erratic behavior had seen her lose more than one important contract. 

He clicked his pen thoughtfully. Zara was well-known for her intricate designs and elaborate fabric work, often using scissors and needles, objects commonly found in her toolkit. It didn't take a seasoned detective to figure out that, with enough motivation, any of these objects could be easily reshaped into a makeshift weapon. 

Winston took another sip of his coffee, rubbing his temples. He looked again at the CCTV recording of Zara. She seemed on edge, showing the typical nervous energy of someone under the influence of drugs. He remembered Zara from a case a year ago- a dispute with a rival designer. She had improved her status in the fashion industry immensely since then, but her life clearly had a negative twist.

The library had been filled with people the day Floyd was murdered. Zara, on five separate occasions, was caught on the CCTV entering and exiting the library. Floyd was no different, he also spent a majority of his day there, lost between the shelves of literature. Winston thought back to his initial conversation with his colleagues about the case: something didn't feel right.

"You said Zara often works with sharp tools, right?" Winston asked the officer taking notes. 

"Yes, scissors, needles... she says they give her the precision she needs for her work." The officer replied, looking up from her notepad. 

Winston knew he had a long day of investigating ahead. With one last glance at the CCTV footage, he left his office prepared to find the truth.

When Letti's lifeless body is found horrifically mutilated by a machete at a secluded mountain cabin, gritty Detective Winston faces a chilling whodunit featuring suspects Delilah and Eddie.

Gazing out at the tranquil scenery of the mountain cabin where Letti met her end, detective Winston pondered the information before him. He had another interview to conduct, and as the mountain breeze tousled his rigid hair, he couldn't help but be reminded of this case's unnerving details.

Eddie was an interesting character, to say the least. A musician of sorts, he was known for incorporating tricks using a machete into his performances. A peculiar stage craft that Winston couldn't begin to comprehend. Performing such stunts would require him to practice, possibly during his free time he spent camping on the outskirts of the city, with his trusted machete always by his side.

The mountain cabin reverberated with somber silence as Winston approached Eddie. He had been staying at the same cabin, having been invited by Letti for a song recording. It was reported that during his stay that Eddie had no other engagements to attend to; an oddity given that this time of year was bustling with music festivals.

"How's the stay been, Eddie?" Winston began, trying to ease Eddie into the conversation.

"Quiet," Eddie responded, his gaze drifting off into the vast span of the desolate mountainscape. "Just how I like it, you know. Helps with the creativity." 

There was an aromatic air to Eddie, of someone who had worked tirelessly to uphold their image in the light of public scrutiny. It was well-known that Eddie was sensitive about his image, keen to maintain the rising trajectory of his music career, a career he held close to his heart.

The cabin’s solitude was a stark reminder of what was at stake for Eddie. Letti, the soulful songbird she was, had managed to unravel a hidden part of Eddie's life that threatened to shatter the glass tower he had been building over the years: his secret drug addiction. Unfortunately, the discovery gave Letti the leverage to manipulate Eddie's successful music career.

Winston kept an attentive poker face while internally connecting the pieces of information.

"The thing is, Eddie," Winston began, his tone sober, "Letti wouldn't have invited you over for any ordinary recording."

"I know," Eddie sighed heavily before he added, "She held my career in her hands, detective."

His confession resounded through the empty cabin, the once picturesque view from the window shading into a grim canvas of their situation. With no one around for miles, Winston wondered what influence this isolation could have on the psyche of the person who was here.

"I reckon we meet again, detective," Eddie said, his voice just above a whisper, as Winston left the cabin.

Detective Winston pulled his car up to the secluded cabin. His visit was to Delilah, the godmother of the recently slain Letti. So far, the only evidence he had found was a machete, smeared with blood.

He knocked on the heavy oak door of her abode and Delilah greeted him with a passive stare. Before he could utter a word, she gestured him inside and they both sat down to chat. Delilah, interestingly, made it a point to hang her machete over the fireplace, “Papa taught me to handle a machete since I was teen. I live out here alone in the wilderness, y'know, just as precaution.” she justified.

Their conversation flowed smoothly until Winston asked Delilah about her past. Instantly, the woman fell silent, her gaze fixed on a spot on the wall, as if she was lost in thought. She curtly responded, "I had a normal, happy childhood. That's all." Winston was struck by this as he knew from others' accounts that no one had ever heard her talk about her childhood or school days in detail.

Winston decided not to probe further, giving Delilah space to guide the conversation. This led her to casually mention her skills with a machete. Come to think of it, she’d won several local machete handling competitions. "I practice regularly," she added, a briefly proud glint in her eyes.

Winston nodded in acknowledgment, his mind returning to documents found in Letti’s possession. These documents seemed to implicate Delilah in some illegal activities. Letti reiteratively voiced concern about her godmother's activities. In fact, she had directly confronted Delilah about the evidence she’d stumbled upon. Even more alarmingly, Letti had confided in her friends about her intention to go public with this evidence.

Letti’s friends shared with Winston how she was deeply worried about Delilah's suspicious activities; however, the specific details of her past remained obscured. Winston took a last glance at the machete hanging over the fireplace before leaving the cabin, a sense of unsettling curiosity lingering in his mind.

Target case file:

In the eerie silence of a moonlit swamp, Leroy's life was gruesomely ended by a sai, setting the stage for Detective Winston's most perplexing murder investigation yet, with suspects Clayton and Madelyn cloaked in mystery.

It was a sweltering summer afternoon when Detective Winston strolled into the local martial arts store. The store owner welcomed Winston with a smile, "Can I help you? Looking to step out of that detective uniform and into a martial arts gi?"

"No," Winston chuckled, "Here on business. Trying to find some information about a pair of sai that was purchased from here." 

The owner furrowed his brow, "Well, many people come in here to buy sai's. Hard to remember them all."

"How about a tall woman, brunette, goes by the name Madelyn?" Winston inquired.

"Madelyn... oh, she's a personal trainer focused on martial arts. She bought a pair of sai's from me a while ago. Saw her practicing with it at the local gym once," The owner shared more," I heard her talking about trusting a few close friends who ended up betraying her, which was tough on her."

Winston decided it was time to pay Madelyn a visit. 

Upon arrival at the gym, Winston spotted Madelyn in the middle of a training session. As he approached, he overheard Madelyn and Leroy, one of her clients with whom she has regular conversations, talking. "Didn't you used to train with Leroy out at the swamp?" her partner asked, catching his breath in-between sets. 

"Yeah, I did. We frequented the swamp for some outdoor training. But he told me he was thinking about changing trainers. Last I saw him, he mentioned heading out to the swamp and planned to meet with my rival for confidential conversations," Madelyn replied, not seeming disturbed by the topic.

Just then a phone rang. Leroy smiled apologetically at Madelyn whose eyes slightly doubt those smiles. He excused himself and moved to a corner of the gym but still in sight of Madelyn. Leroy talked over the phone with a certain intensity. Winston overheard the conversation and realized that it was Madelyn's rival on the other end.

Just as Winston approached Madelyn, she finished demonstrating an exemplary sai technique to her current client. The conversation he'd overheard and Madelyn's evidently skillful handling of the sai intrigued him. 

He introduced himself and asked for a few minutes of her time. She obliged, accompanying him to a quieter corner of the gym. "You've been training Leroy for the past few months, correct?"

Madelyn's eyes flickered a hint of surprise, "Yes, I have. Why do you ask?"

"No special reason. Just trying to figure out a few things," Winston replied calmly. He was mindful not to let any suspicions arise. He noted that Madelyn seemed to be aware of Leroy's conversation with her rival and that she was around the vicinity that day. He vaguely recalled something about Leroy planning to ditch Madelyn as his trainer.

Winston left the gym with a budding curiosity, wondering about Madelyn's past friendships and betrayals. He had heard through the grapevine and now firsthand from the store owner about Madelyn being betrayed in the past by close friends. Winston knew better than most, that old wounds sometimes pushed people over the edge. He made a quick mental note to follow up on this lead the next chance he got.

Winston gazed at the murky waters of the swamp crime scene. The grim sight of Leroy's untimely demise probing him to dig deep. He knew none of this was circumstantial, and his insistence on finding what happened was building momentum. Beginning to question Clayton, Winston quickly turned to the night of the crime.

"Where were you when this happened, Clayton?" Instead of answering directly, Clayton sidestepped the question with whereabouts deflections, "The swamp is big, detective, could be anywhere...You know my work, survival training and all that." 

Moving to Clayton being a local swamp guide, he touted the detective with a bravado that didn't quite sit well. Winston had seen him many times before, on those survival tours he hosted, slogging around in the swamp like a kid in the rain. A man of many faces, all too familiar with this swamp.

"Always visiting this swamp alone, Clayton? Even on the day of the murder?" Winston demanded, his coy glance cut through Clayton's unease. "Just my daily routine… and solitude helps me cope," Clayton barely admitted, implying he spent the entire day of the murder alone.

Taking his investigation to the local tavern, Winston mused over the conversations he'd had with the patrons. Clayton leaving the bar, alone, around the time of the crime was a constant motif he couldn't shake off. The ever resentful, Clayton, skulking into his car at night etched a picture hard to ignore.

While unraveling the connection between Clayton and a known criminal, a top regular directed Winston to a corner of the bar, "Detective, see there...Clayton with that damn felon, always hissing back and forth." Winston couldn’t decipher what they said, but the veil surrounding their hushed conversations disturbed him.

Moreover, Clayton's complex love life added to the intrigues. The quick switch in ex-wife's love from Clayton to Leroy, followed by a swift marriage had wounded Clayton. His love for her was clear, and Leroy, well, he was a barrier to their possible reconciliation. A small-town rumor that his ex-wife was so taken with Leroy that she had exclaimed, "I won't even think about patching things up with Clayton as long as Leroy is around!" ensured Clayton had real reasons to begrudge Leroy. 

The evening came to an end with Winston feeling no closer to a resolution. He exited the bar, his thoughts jumbled with images of a vengeful Clayton, an infatuated, criminal whispering, and the memory of a solitary figure in the murky swamp, evasive responses hanging in the air. His quest for justice uncompromising, as he slipped into the night, the puzzle still seemed incomplete.
question: Who is the most likely murderer?

context:
Background files from related investigations (some may be irrelevant):

When Mack's life got fatally bleached out on a soccer field, it was up to Detective Winston to sift through the dark clues left by his suspects: Helen and Danielle.

Winston stared at the crime scene in front of him. The soccer field's lush greenery was marred by the gruesome sight of Mack's lifeless body. His bleached face was contorted in an expression of surprise, as though he couldn't believe what had happened.

"Helen, did you clean up post-game?" Winston posed his question with a stern expression. The corner of his mouth upturned as he noticed a potential clue, but didn’t let it reach his eyes.

"Yes, Detective. As I always do," Helen replied, her face drawn with somberness. Winston noted her impeccably clean appearance and gloves, without a trace of mud despite the weather and her outdoor responsibilities.

Helen was the housekeeper here. Mack, having no family, had entrusted her with the keys to the house, as mentioned in his will. Winston flipped through his notes, recalling that not only did Helen work for Mack, but she came to the game early that day and was still there after everyone had left, right around the time Mack was found dead.

Winston delved a little deeper. "I understand that you enjoy camping, Helen...alone?" 

"Yes, it's my chance to unwind, to hike off trails and be amongst nature. Besides, I enjoy the solitude that these trips offer and prefer not to have any company," Helen added, thereby hinting at why she refused to let anyone join her on these outings.

"I see," Winston said. "And water activities, do you engage in any during these camping trips?"

Taken aback, Helen never expected such a question. "Actually, no. I don't fancy spending time near the water, camping is mostly about the solitude for me."

"Hmm, I see." Winston made a show of jotting this down in his notebook, his eyes never leaving Helen's face.

"The people at the house, do they appreciate your work?" Winston posed his question carefully.

"I’ve overheard malicious conversations about me and my work. It feels...almost humiliating, and objectifying. It hurt to know that the people I care for don’t return the sentiment,” Helen admitted, looking away.

The detective carefully observed Helen, making no judgments. As more pieces clicked into place, he thanked Helen and excused her, promising to update her further on the case. Winston prided himself on his professionalism. His job was simply to collect clues for an often unforgiving puzzle.

He couldn't shake the thought of why a housekeeper, like Helen, who strongly avoided mud and water, went camping so frequently, choosing often to go off the beaten trail. Equally intriguing was her insistence on not allowing others to accompany her on these trips. Hence, he moved on to collecting the next piece of the puzzle, all the while, carefully observing every action, every reaction, and every telltale indicator of deception. The game was still afoot, and Winston would leave no stone unturned.

Detective Winston rubbed his temples, staring at the contents strewn from his bulging file. The victim's name was Mack. The young man had been on the cusp of marriage, though rumors swirled that the engagement was nothing more than an elaborate ruse to satisfy the expectations of his parents.

Winston sighed deeply and continued to scan the case file. There was something unusual about this crime. The murder weapon of choice, a bottle of bleach, was anything but typical, and the name Danielle, scribbled repeatedly throughout his notes, gave the detective pause.

Danielle - a local spiritual guru known throughout the community for her meticulous cleaning. Winston found it curious that someone who used cleanliness as a tool to attain spirituality would find herself mixed up in this grisly case. 

From what the detective had gathered, Danielle had been conducting one of her renowned spiritual sessions the day Mack was killed and with a chilling thought, Winston remembered that Mack could have been one of the attendees. After all, the soccer field where the young man's life was snuffed out was also Danielle's usual haunt for leading her sessions. In fact, she had the whole city at her fingertips, but she always chose the ever-bustling soccer field - a fact he couldn’t dismiss lightly.

Danielle was a fervent believer in spiritual purity and she saw Mack's loveless marriage as a direct threat to that purity. That much was clear to Winston from copious notes and conversations he uncovered. He recalled one particular conversation recorded between Danielle and a friend where, talking about Mack, she had stated fervently, "He needs to remain single. Marriage without love would be catastrophic to his spiritual purity". 

Church conversations known city-wide revealed Mack was ready to be shackled in a loveless marriage, a reality the entire city was privy to. This caught Winston's attention. He was certain Danielle was aware of Mack's arrangement, and it was playing into her concept of purity. This notion was definitely worth exploring.

The curious case of Danielle continued as Winston flicked through the file. Her obsessive cleaning ticked another in a list of oddities surrounding this spiritual guru. Bleach was her go-to choice, and she dedicated her spare time to scrubbing every surface she could reach, her way of achieving external and internal purity - or so she claimed. 

Winston shook his head as he closed the case file, a heavy sigh spewing from his lips. He had more questions now than when he'd started. Danielle’s belief system, her ubiquitous presence at the soccer field, Mack's loveless marriage, and Danielle's passion for cleaning - they all lay like jigsaw puzzle pieces yearning to be fit together. But how? The question remained unanswered as he rose from his seat, his thoughts lost in the intricate web of the case that lay before him.

When fitness enthusiast Uma is ominously murdered with a vial of acid at her local gym, it's up to seasoned Detective Winston to unravel the mystery between the two prime suspects, Irving and Addison.

Detective Winston sat hunched over the cold steel counter in the diner, specks of rain slowly dripping onto the vinyl seat from his coat. He absently flipped through the case file of Uma, somehow the atmosphere matching the mournful story he was reading.

According to the notes, Uma was a trainer and part-time script consultant at the same fitness center where Irving, the suspect, also trained. Both typically scheduled their workouts late in the evening, customarily ending when the gym was mostly vacant. The evening Uma met her untimely demise, irrefutable evidence shows Irving stayed later than she did, apparently relishing the solitude. The stark lighting of the closed gym only added to the chilly atmosphere.

Winston carefully sipped his coffee, the bitter taste pulling him from his reverie. Grabbing his notepad, he jotted down a few points to discuss with Irving. Apart from his regular gym routine, various aspects of his writing career were catching Winston's eye.

Irving was known for his precise work on scripts, specifically for his detailed research into harmful substances, even down to their handling and utilization. His alarmingly realistic work had earned him a strange kind of reputation, though no one could deny it fascinated viewers.

Given this, Uma’s claim that Irving stole her work didn’t seem so far off. Looking closely at her file again, Winston found a direct threat from Uma stating she would expose Irving's deception to the public. It seemed like this plagiarism accusation had Irving on edge, a tension that seemed to whisper of something dangerous. 

Heading out of the diner, Winston decided to head over to Irving’s apartment. It was a short drive, the buildings looming against the gloomy sky forebodingly, each window alight as though the eyes of some unseen spectators.

As he approached the building, he recalled a report of Irving carrying a vial from his car to his apartment. The vial itself seemed ordinary but combined with his previous online purchases of corrosive substances from a store, it painted a grim picture.

Upon reaching the apartment, his observational skills kicked in, the detective noting the absence of lights; Irving had not yet returned home. His mind wandered back to the fitness center, and the reports claiming that Irving usually stayed late rang even truer considering the current time.

"Hey, Winston," barked a voice over the phone, pulling him back to reality. 

"Irving went home, got caught in the morning traffic. You guess what he drove?"

Winston sighed, the picture painfully clear. "I'm guessing it was a car."

"Well, today's just full of surprises for you, innit? Yeah, it was the car," the officer on the other line chuckled before he hung up.

Winston leaned against the chilling wall, thoughts whirling around in his mind, the proverbially web becoming denser with each passing moment. Irving had a lot to answer for, and that included what happened the tragic night Uma was murdered.

Winston squinted at the digital clock on his car's dashboard; it was 7 p.m., Uma's workout time, the hour at which the tragedy had unfolded. Winston seemed to have developed a knack for piecing together the minutiae of his victim's lives, to the point he often found himself involved in their routines. Not too far from Uma's favourite treadmills, he could see Addison, Uma's personal trainer, putting another client through his paces. 

"I heard about Uma." The trace of guilt was ever so subtle in Addison's voice. 

"I suppose you were her trainer?" Winston asked, casually observing the gym. 

"Yes, Uma had a steady workout routine. Four times a week, without fail." Addison seemed to be avoiding his gaze, focusing on tidying up some equipment round. "It was during my work hours and we had a well-set regimen. It never changed. Not even on the day she was killed."

As Winston took note of the gym's patrons and its facilities, he noticed the safe was situated in such a way that it was visible to the entire room. There was a sign that read, 'No unauthorized access.' Winston, however, recalled something from the case file about Addison being seen taking money from the said safe.

Arriving back at his office, Winston rifled through his jacket pocket for his notes. As he scanned the document for his key points he remembered Addison had recently caught the gym's attention... and not for his training talent. Apparently, money had begun to disappear from the gym's safe after Addison started working there, around the same time Uma found out about some theft.

Looking over the notes, Winston couldn't ignore the fact that none of Addison's training sessions took him to distant locations. They were all locally based, suggesting that the man had absolutely no need to travel out of town. However, according to the evidence, Addison purchased several items out of the locality, paying in cash to avoid the money being traced. Winston wondered if it was from the same cash that was disappearing from the gym's safe?

It was getting late, and the detective had had his fill of theories for one day. He decided it was time for some shut-eye, hoping that a good night's rest would help him unravel the mystery he found himself steeped in.

Target case file:

"In the gritty underworld of professional wrestling, Jim's life ends abruptly on the mat with a bottle of bleach; now, it's up to Detective Winston to grapple with suspects, Clyde and Roxanne, to uncover the truth."

Winston scrutinized the crime scene once more, the wrestling ring where Jim had met a grisly end. The potent scent of bleach hung heavily in the air, a sensation that left a harsh taste in Winston's mouth. The smell was familiar - an offensive olfactory signature that he associated with one man, Clyde, a plumber known by his colleagues for frequently incorporating bleach into his work as part of his cleaning regimen.

His next stop was Clyde's regular haunt, the local union of plumbers. As Winston walked in, he spotted Clyde, his sketchbook in hand, a common sight in his daily life where he was seen everywhere with it - even the park, where pedestrians would note his unmistakable silhouette sketching in the fading sunset.

"Morning, Clyde," Winston greeted. The burly plumber acknowledged him while carefully retrieving something from his bag. 

"Yeah?" Clyde retorted, his ever-present sketchbook peeking from the crevice of his well-worn bag.

"I see you've got that sketchbook of yours." Winston gestured, the sketchbook already a topic of many conversations among Clyde's colleagues.

"Yes," Clyde held it up. "I just came from the park. Sketched some people. Most were oblivious."

"Something to keep your mind at ease, right?" Winston deduced, knowing Clyde's odd habits from previous conversations.

“Exactly! I've been a fan of sketching ever since my first ex-girlfriend. Helped me cope with my... possessiveness," Clyde admitted, his underlying nature painting a clearer picture to Winston.

Winston subtly noticed Clyde’s clothing reeking of bleach, a plumbing prerequisite that often resulted in him leaving work, smelling like he'd just scrubbed down a newly cleaned bathroom.

“Would you know anything about Jim?” Winston directed the conversation, veering away from Clyde's routine.

Clyde's mood shifted subtly, “Yeah, my recent ex. She’s now with him... Jim." Clyde confessed, his voice bitter as he recalled the numerous occasions he'd been witness to Jim's overly familiar and openly flirtatious demeanor with his ex, a sight he forcefully ignored, especially when he was sketching in the park.

"Your ex? The very one who confirmed she was dating Jim?" Winston asked, dubiously.

“Yeah, she left me for him… Jim, who enjoyed making a spectacle of himself, openly flirting with her in public. Hard to miss when you're watching.” Clyde admitted, referring to when he was seen spying on Jim and his ex-girlfriend recently.

"Well, better safe than sorry,” Winston responded, cleverly implying his knowledge of Clyde's recent surveillance antics.

“Exactly," Clyde quietly concurred, before falling silent.

“Alright, Clyde. Thanks for your time.” Winston stood to leave, a wave of vigilante justice washing over him as he exited the plumbers union, leaving Clyde to his sketching, an activity his union peers had noticed often happened on his days off.

Deep in his office at the local precinct, Detective Winston sifted through the crime scene photos again. Jim, a well-known wrestling hero, was now just another file sitting on his desk. The cause of death - bleach poisoning.

Switching on his computer, Winston pulled up the latest piece of evidence - a CCTV footage from a nearby pharmacy. There, he saw Roxanne, a persistent critic of Jim's wrestling tactics, making a purchase. The timestamp on the video showed the same day of Jim's tragic demise.

Winston got up, deciding to pay Roxanne a visit. On getting to her place, he saw her retrieving a ticket to a wrestling match from one of her drawers. The date matched the one on the pharmacy’s CCTV.

"Hi, Roxanne. Nice place you've got here," Winston began.

"Thank you. Detective right? How can I help you?" Roxanne replied.

"Just a few questions. You went to Jim's match, correct?"

"Yeah, I retrieved this ticket from my drawer this morning. Wanted to see if his moves had improved."

Winston was quite intrigued, "As a nurse, what brings you to wrestling matches? Not your usual night out, I assume?"

"No detective. It’s purely professional. Being a fan of the sport, I had some... let's say disagreements with Jim's wrestling. In fact, I have quite frequently denounced his techniques during our gym sessions."

Winston nodded. Back at the station, he found a lot of hate speech addressed at Jim online, written under Roxanne's username. He also found her search history that showed she had been researching about bleach poisoning. This woman had been openly critical of Jim. Some members of the wrestling community even regarded her criticism as a hate crime against wrestlers.

"Was the wrestling match good?" Winston asked out of the blue.

"It was the usual stuff. Jim's techniques bore me. I even told him so a couple of times at the gym, but he never would listen."

Intrigued by her choice of words, Winston subtly added, "Yeah, his techniques seem to draw in the crowds, nonetheless. He was getting quite famous attending all these major matches."

"No doubt about that," she replied.

"And you made a 'stop' before heading to the wrestling match?" Winston asked casually.

"Stop? Oh, you mean the pharmacy. Had to get some household supplies, including a bottle of bleach," she explained.

Winston watched her as she spoke. He'd done a quick check before he came. There were no reported thefts of bleach in the surrounding area and this made sense. Roxanne, with her nursing background, didn't need to steal it. She had all the knowledge she needed, right at her fingertips, including how to use bleach as a…poison?

Exiting her home, Winston decided to return to the precinct. He had a lot of evidence to sift through, including the evidences that showed Roxanne had been openly critical of Jim at their gym and her online research history about bleach poisoning. But it's not his job to make conclusions, or was it?
question: Who is the most likely murderer?

"In the gritty underworld of professional wrestling, Jim's life ends abruptly on the mat with a bottle of bleach; now, it's up to Detective Winston to grapple with suspects, Clyde and Roxanne, to uncover the truth."

Winston squinted at the wrestling ticket stashed away in an evidence bag, blew a puff of smoke, and looked at the date again. It was the same day Jim, the famous wrestler, had been murdered. He snuffed out his cigarette, pocketed the ticket, and made his way toward his interview with Roxanne.

He found Roxanne nursing a cup of tea in a spacious apartment, its décor tinged with layers of transient life. Among various moving boxes, catching his attention were the remnants of a ticket in a drawer, aligning precisely with the one he pocketed, indicating it had been retrieved from there before the event. He noticed a handful of discarded sim cards on the table, each from a different carrier, indicating she had likely changed her phone number several times.

“Roxanne, is it?” Winston began. His words were met with a curt nod.

"That wrestling match ticket I found at your place, you attended the same event that Jim did, didn’t you?" Winston pushed the evidence bag toward Roxanne. She had meticulously planned to attend this wrestling show, as evidenced by the ticket fragments in her drawer.

She squared her shoulders and admitted, "Yes, I'm a big fan of wrestling, and Jim always attracted the crowd."

Flicking through his notes, Winston proceeded. "Looks like you work in healthcare, Roxanne, a nurse, correct?"

With a tad of confusion etched on her face, Roxanne admitted as such.

Despite her career, Winston saw her adeptness in subjects beyond her field. She had done her fair share of questionable research, she knew bleach could be a useful tool, not just for cleaning. Winston received a tip-off about her internet search history pointing toward research on bleach poisoning.

He decided to dig a little deeper. "At the pharmacy, where you bought the bleach, the CCTV footage showed you making that purchase." He let her know how he came across the information. Her flinch of surprise was hard to miss.

Snowballing into more dire topics, Winston mentioned a recent spat taking place on her front lawn. Roxanne's family had heatedly argued with her. "Your family has been trying to reach you," Winston gestured towards the stack of letters in the corner.

Sighing, Roxanne admitted that things had escalated until she left the location in a huff, ignoring repeated attempts by her family to get back in touch. 

"No neighbors. I move... a lot," Roxanne confessed, changing the topic. 

Winston frowned. He needed to know why there were no reports of stolen bleach near pharmacies surrounding both the wrestling arena and Roxanne's current residence. But he decided to leave that for another time.

On his way out, Winston muttered a quiet "thank you" before he left Roxanne to her solitude. As he departed, he stole one last glance at the stacks of unopened letters sitting forlornly in the corner. There was an awful lot to unravel here, it seemed. Yet, as always, Winston knew the truth was buried somewhere, waiting to be unearthed.

Winston had spent the day visiting the wrestling ring where Jim’s body had been found. As the man responsible for orchestrating the match, including assigning responsibilities to the referees, the matter had naturally become deeply personal to Clyde. Not to mention, he was a plumber and was therefore in a kind of position that made it hard for people to not remember him. The wrestling match was held late at night, when he could manage time from his job, and it just so happened that most people had already left for their homes by the end of it. Winston remembered seeing Jim flirting openly with Clyde's ex-girlfriend during the event. It was a sight hard to forget. He picked up his camera bag, preparing for the night’s task. It wouldn't be pretty, but it was necessary.

Winston decided to ask Clyde about the match first, "What are the criteria for a good referee in the match, Clyde?" The question was a simple icebreaker.

Clyde shrugged, looking at Winston with a puzzled look. "Well... referees need to control the wrestlers, redirect their energy if it goes astray. Also, they have the responsibility to overlook the match, ensure that it runs smooth and everyone plays by the rules."

Meeting with the burly plumber, who also moonlighted as the wrestling match organizer, was a step that needed to occur. He was seen leaving the ring after the night's wrestling events with Jim. It was a fact that couldn't be simply glanced over.

Winston, with a voice steady as a rock asked, "A tad unusual, Clyde, you two leaving together. Was it not?"

Clyde shifted uncomfortably, "Naw, detective. It was late, and most folks had already gone home. Just tidyin' up, you know."

"Is that so?" Winston replied. Clyde’s bleach-streaked work clothes were a testament to his plumbing job. Always smelling strongly of bleach. "And don’t plumbers often use bleach for cleaning purposes?" Winston emphasised his point.

A shrug from Clyde gave Winston the satisfaction of confirmation. "It's got plenty uses, detective. And yeah, a good clean ain't possible without some bleach."

His coworkers could vouch for his frequent bleach-infused work clothes. A distinct, eye-watering odor. Winston recognized it as he walked towards him. Yes, he couldn't ignore the strong smell of bleach.

Instead of pushing the issue, Winston decided to turn the conversation towards Clyde’s past. He had treated his ex-girlfriends more like possessions than partners and had recently been seen spying on Jim and his ex-girlfriend - a woman Jim had been openly flirting with at the wrestling matches and who had confirmed that she was now dating Jim.

"Clyde," Winston began, all seriousness, "we got reports of you looking into Jim and his... interests, other than wrestling, can you shed some light on that?"

Clyde shifted again, "Well, detective, that ain't nothing but...but concern, you see, for my ex."

Winston simply nodded, staying silent. He had to stay neutral, had to listen to both sides of the story before he could make his conclusion. And that's exactly what he did. Letting Clyde make his explanation, was it concern or possessiveness camouflaged? Perhaps a bit of both. It was a tangled web, one Winston was sure to unravel eventually.

In the shimmering opulence of a luxury restaurant, Roderick's life was abruptly ended by a pistol's merciless blow; now Detective Winston must untangle the web of Oscar and Brianna's testimonies.

Detective Winston, staring at the rain streaming down his office window, absentmindedly stirred his lukewarm coffee. Another murder landed on his desk. The victim, Roderick. The list of facts pertaining to Brianna, a tenacious teacher suspected to be involved, seemed to be a never-ending stream of potential leads.

Sifting through stacks of evidence, he came across a statement from Roderick, Brianna's boss, refusing to consider her for a promotion at work. Winston placed it on top of the pile as he planned his approach. The next piece of evidence was a statement from a valet at the luxury restaurant. According to the valet, not only did both Brianna and Roderick dine there on the night of the murder, but they were also both seen leaving the restaurant at the same time.

Winston made his way over to the shooting range. A police report detailed that a pistol Brianna recently purchased and practiced with here was identical to the one used to kill Roderick. 

The shooting range was winding down for the evening. Winston was able to speak to the range officer, "So, Brianna's been coming here often?"

"Yeah, she's really dedicated. You wouldn't believe it but she's won several competitions here," the range officer commented, leading Winston to the lanes where Brianna often practiced.

Within his stack of evidence, Winston found a copy of the restaurant's reservation list, confirming Brianna's presence at Classico's that night. More evidence from his stack showed that Brianna had been ambitiously seeking the same promotion at the school she worked, the promotion Roderick instead received.

He soon found himself speaking with the restaurant staff. The valet, waitstaff, and even some kitchen staff all recalled seeing Brianna leave the restaurant around the same time as Roderick. Most interestingly, they all bore witness to an argument that Brianna had with Roderick during dinner.

Next, Winston stopped by the school where Roderick worked. A fellow teacher revealed how deeply disappointed Brianna was when Roderick got the promotion instead of her.

With the collected evidence, Winston knew he needed to confront Brianna. 

"We've talked to the range officer at the shooting range," said Winston, meeting Brianna in her classroom.

Brianna nodded, "Yes, I spill my frustrations on paper targets, helps me to stay focused."

"Do you dine at Classico's often," Winston asked casually.

"Yes, once every so often," replied Brianna, "I’m a regular there."

"I’m sure they recognized you the night Roderick was killed," Winston said, subtly sliding the copy of the reservations list across the desk. 

"I suppose," Brianna said, cleaning her glasses, "But isn’t it a little strange that a busy detective like you is asking about dinner plans?”

Winston shrugged and stood up. "Well, duty calls. It was nice chatting with you, Brianna." Making his leave, Winston thought about all the pieces he had gathered and how they all seemed to point to Brianna.

Winston was nursing a black coffee and flipping through the case file when the first cracks of dawn speckled the dreary sky. The victim, Roderick, had been a stand-up entrepreneur before he caught a bullet. Roderick had agreed to meet his husband, Oscar, to discuss their divorce plans on the day he died. 

"Why flee when you're already getting a divorce?" Winston found himself murmuring to his empty, scarcely lit office. A note from a confidential source in the case file revealed that Oscar had heard from Roderick that he was planning to leave him. 

Winston's musings were interrupted by a phone call. It was Oscar's son, Josh. He cheerfully announced his excitement about the languid summer that lay ahead of him, spent at home. Winston rubbed his eyes, cracked his back, and decided it was time to pay Oscar a visit.

Oscar lived in a modest suburban home. The early morning dew lightly wet the sidewalk and the chill hung in the air. His silver sedan with premium rims was parked in the driveway, just as Oscar's neighbor had mentioned. She'd been seeing their car parked there with the windows down at all times lately. Upon inspection, Winston could see a receipt for a large, black suitcase on the passenger seat. He made a note of it.

Oscar, on the other hand, looked like a shadow of his former self. Tired eyes, unkempt hair, and the flicker of sadness in his eyes confirmed his ongoing love for Roderick, despite everything. The sad fact that he had been forced to say goodbye to his job a month ago only added to his woe. His therapist had been supporting him through the divorce-related depression, but with Roderick's sudden demise, things had taken a turn for the worse.

Winston was offered a cup of coffee while he casually asked Oscar about the night of Roderick's death. Oscar offered up the information that he had proposed a toast at the private party right before Roderick was shot, diverting everyone's attentions momentarily away from the man. After having his fill of the tepid liquid, Winston got up, thanked Oscar for his time, and walked back towards his car.

The sound of his shoes crunching the freshly dewed gravel, Winston lit up a cigarette. He drove away eventually, leaving Oscar in his rearview mirror, standing in the doorway. He gave an inward groan thinking about the mountain of paperwork waiting for him at the station.

In this mess, a voice echoed in his head, 'Heard Oscar was in therapy. Depression, they said.' 

It was a long day and Winston was certain, it was going to be a long case.

In the quiet isolation of a remote chalet, Cecilia's life brutally ended by an axe and it's now up to the jaded Detective Winston to untangle a web of deceit involving suspects, Stuart and Alice.

Winston wrinkled his now weather-beaten brow, his dark eyes hard and focused as he stood at the outskirts of the secluded chalet. The sight of Cecilia's body, found long after the time Stuart was noted alone at the site lent a sense of unease that still imprinted in his mind from the crime scene photos.

There was a strange quiet that persisted in the area as the evening shadows coalesced further into night. Winston was particularly interested in the electrical works of the chalet, the severed power cables indicative of Stuart’s well-known method of using his axe to cut them. All conveniently hidden behind walls and ceilings but paramount in their purpose. He was reminded that important clues sometimes lurk in the most innocuous of places.

Winston glanced around, his gaze settling on Stuart lumbering towards him. As usual, the man had his tool bag over one sturdy shoulder, the familiar shape of an axe imprinted onto its side. Its weight was seemingly imprinted onto Stuart’s posture, yet worn with a sense of profound solidarity. A sense of familiarity, born from years of dedication to his profession and the meticulous demand for his specialized tools, such as axes.

“Stuart?” Winston enquired, attempting to mirror a casual air.

“Yeah, that would be me,” Stuart responded, his respect for the detective's powerful presence evident.

“You've been working on this property?”

“Sure have,” the large man nodded, setting his tool bag into the dirt nearby. The soft clink of tools echoed faintly in the silent expanse. Stuart was a proficient electrician, everyone in the county knew. He had harbored resentment against Cecilia, for reasons unknown; a motive that lingered with a subtle hint in the air. His rigor and loyalty to his profession manifested in every job site he touched—an axe always included in his equipment.

A long moment passed, the evening wind whistling in the background. 

"Cecilia, the owner... she hired you, didn't she?" Winston broke the silence, his gaze firm on Stuart.

“Yeah... had a bad power outage that day."

"How long did it last?"

"Unusual one. Lasted all day actually."

The chirping of crickets began to build and a layer of frost was slowly painting itself across the chalet’s exterior. This suggested that there were no other workers or inhabitants during the time of Stuart's work.

Winston found himself hooked onto the echo of Stuart's resounding words, stirring question after question in his mind. He wouldn’t voice them; not yet. 

A cold wind blew past the duo, shifting leaves rustled around the chalet whispering secrets that they had witnessed. A secret Winston had set out to uncover. With that, he bid Stuart a goodnight and left the chalet site, the outline of the crime scene etched into his memory as he sped off into the distance; his wearied sights set on tomorrow's set of questions.

Detective Winston sat in his office, a thick folder splayed open in front of him. Inside were various reports about a school counselor named Alice. Alice was evidently no ordinary school counselor - a slew of allegations and complications surrounded her. 

Winston got up, tucked the folder under his arm and headed to the school where Alice was employed.

As he approached the counselor's office, he could hear the muffled sound of murmuring in the hallway around him. A little bird had earlier mentioned that Cecilia had tripped over Alice’s secret of a grade-changing scandal and had evidence of her infamous extramarital affair. 

As Winston left Alice’s office, he knew the web was much more tangled than what met the eye.

In the heart of a brawling wrestling ring, Cecil lay lifeless, a bullet his final opponent, marking the onset of a complex investigation for Detective Winston with suspects Tiffany and Theresa under the spotlight.

As Winston took a sip from his thermos, he couldn't help but feel an eerie sense of familiarity around the crime scene. The murder had taken place in a wrestling ring, and Winston had a connection with the victim, Cecil.

Winston decided to pay a visit to Theresa, a flower girl, and a recent ex-girlfriend of Cecil. She lived alone, in a house far from the usual hustle and bustle of the city. Winston noticed the extraordinary silence that surrounded her home; no visitors and probably no witnesses.

As he waited for her to answer the door, he noticed a course completion certificate for gun safety framed on her wall. It was dated last year.

"Interesting," he muttered to himself, knocking once more. 

Her mother, a police officer herself, opened the door. Winston quickly introduced himself and asked for Theresa. It was while they waited together for Theresa, the mother casually mentioned how she pushed Theresa to take a gun safety course when she borrowed her off-duty pistol for protection purposes.

Theresa was a regular at the local park, where Winston managed to find her later that day. He was surprised to see her all alone in the green expanse, devoid of any human interaction. 

"Evening Theresa," Winston started. 

She glanced towards him, and Winston could see the emotional upheaval in her eyes. "Bad day?"

"A lot of those, recently," she confessed and Winston noted how Cecil's recent break-up with her had her on an edge. He delved into the night of the murder, asking her where she was that evening.

"Well, I uh... I found myself at the wrestling ring that night. I wasn't in a good place and I... I just needed to see Cecil one last time..."

As she spoke, Winston could sense the heavy emotional burden she was carrying. The mat, the spotlight, and Cecil wrestling that night – it all reminded her of times that once were but would never be again.

As the cold moonlight filtered through the grimy windows onto the still darkened bar, Winston swung open the door. The dim street outside was almost as quiet as the bar. The wrestling ring in the corner of the bar silently reminded Winston of Cecil's tragic end that happened shortly after the last gig.

The bar chairs were turned upside down on the tables, a common practice to signal the closing time for an establishment. As the place was empty, it was clear that Tiffany, the bartender, would have cleaned up after the wrestling match and night's business. Winston remembered hearing from the other staffers how Tiffany was always the last to leave, her commitment ensuring that she was there till the bar was ready for the next day.

Winston couldn't help but remember that, according to the witnesses, Tiffany was still at work even after the wrestling match was over and the bar should've been closed. Winston nodded to himself; this was a violation of the law.

Also, there was talk about Tiffany serving alcohol beyond the mandated hours, to which Cecil himself was privy to. The violation would have been enough to cost Tiffany both her bartender’s license and her job if it reached the right ears. Cecil had planned to expose this, which Winston found interesting. Could this have been the catalyst for the brewing storm?

However, Winston was left without much to say when he found a silver pistol tucked away in one of the storage rooms of the bar. A chill ran down his spine as he recognized that it was the weapon that ended Cecil's life.

"Been doing a bit of spring cleaning?" Winston asked, showing the service permit Tiffany had applied for her concealed carry. A fact usually ignored by regular folks but not by a detective like Winston, "It’s quite a setup you have behind the counter. How often do you get such rowdy patrons that you need to pack heat?"

Tiffany responded, "Only to ensure safety."

Nodding at her reply, Winston continued looking around the bar. He'd been in bars where wrestling matches were held before, but there was a unique allure to this joint. It embraced the rough and tumble nature of such events, welcoming the wrestling matches as part of the nightlife.

"Tiffany, you have an interesting gig,” Winston remarked, “Hosting wrestling matches at the bar, well, given the scene, it does seem fitting.”

Tiffany chuckled slightly at this statement, “I do what I can to keep the doors open detective.”

With that reply, Winston ended his investigations and stepped out into the brisk night, his mind filtering and analyzing the layers of facts and statements. He glanced back at the bar, his gaze falling on Tiffany still behind the counter, alone with the closing rituals.

In the glitzy, high-stakes world of casinos, Jamal meets a deadly end by frog poison, leaving Detective Winston to weave through a web of deceit with two prime suspects - Kimberly and Lillian.

Winston stood somberly over the roulette table, the stilled wheel now a chilling reminder of the danger that lay in the house's favor. Jamal's empty chair, a token of a dangerous gamble. Too high of a stake, with a godchild as your appointed dealer.

"Lillian, was it?" Winston began, attempting to keep his tone as neutral as possible. The woman before him, a young biologist specializing in amphibians, nodded as she squirmed slightly under his gaze.

"Jamal spoke highly of you," he said, casting an eye towards her drink. She gulped, but stayed silent.

"He trusted you," Winston continued, surveying the crime scene with his trained eye. "Even was seen taking a sip from your very drink there."

Lillian straightened in her chair. "Always giving him advice," Winston mused, a thought dancing at the edge of his vision. "And always willing to try something new."

It wasn't hard to guess that Lillian had always desired more. The lust for power hung around her like an exotic perfume, intoxicating to those in her proximity. She wanted to be Jamal. Jamal, the casino mogul; his elusive empire tantalizingly within reach.

Outside, the neon lights of the casino blinked erratically, casting an eerie greenish hue over the scene. A darting shadow caught Winston's attention - a strange silhouette of a rare species of frog in a glass tank, well-known amongst biologists for its lethal toxins, shimmered in the glow. An interesting pet for a woman so consumed with desire.

"Lillian, you're a herpetologist, we gather?" Winston questioned, inclining his head towards the amphibian. She nodded, a glint appearing in her eyes. "And you've been studying the toxins of this frog for years..."

Dismissing Lillian, Winston surveyed the casino once more. It was a den of decadence, a palace of transient prosperity run by Jamal, the giver of fortunes, who had no other known kin but a science-smitten child drawn to the perilous allure of her amphibian pets.

One clear fact remained. Jamal had listened to Lillian and she... well, she was next in line for his throne. This was not a conjecture but a simple fact an observer might note, just as one might notice the inescapable presence of a rare poison frog in Lillian's possession.

As Winston made his exit from the pulsating hub of the casino, his mind turned over the night's events. Lillian, pacing the casino floor, her eyes on Jamal, and Jamal's undying trust in his favored godchild. Pieces of a puzzle waiting to be fit together. But that, he left strictly for the reader to sort out.

Winston straightened his tie, a habitual tick when he was nearing a suspect. Tonight, that meant paying a visit to one Kimberly, a spry octogenarian with a fascination for amphibians one wouldn't normally associate with a grandma.

Walking up the porch, he could see through a dimly lit parlor. There, Kimberly was found, hunched over a substantial amount of research papers sprawled across the room. Winston noticed the frequency of articles related to the extraction and lethality of poison from a particular species of frog.

Knocking gently on the open door, Kimberly straightened, stealthily slipping an exotic-looking frog back into its terrarium, before turning her attention toward the unexpected guest. "Detective Winston," she held out a hand. She was sprightly, yes, but he noted the careful, controlled movements as she moved.

"I heard about your recent acquisition," Winston began, lowering himself onto a lumpen crochet-covered armchair. "Must be quite the conversation starter." He flicked a glance toward the rare frog, one known for having highly toxic qualities.

"Oh, it causes quite the buzz amongst my grandkids," Kimberly chuckled, her eyes twinkling with mirth. "They're scattered in different cities, all of which I've been to at least once, you see. Every time I visit, they share stories about their friends also believing in these new identities I seem to be adopting. First a globetrotter, and now a herpetologist. Quite the adventurous granny I am!"

Winston smiled politely, musing over Kimberly's statement and looking at a family picture, recalling his information about her visits to her grandkids' residences in the different cities. 

The conversation switched topics from frogs to Jamal, a man who Kimberly had a trusted relationship with, and the victim in this case. It was at the casino where Jamal choked on his all-time favorite gin and tonic, his body later identified as being laced with an unhealthy dose of poison.

"I saw you there that night, Kimberly," Winston said with a neutral expression. Kimberly just nodded, neither denying nor admitting to more than was asked.

Once finished, Winston excused himself, heading back to his car. He knew he had to tread lightly; Kimberly was a grandmother, but she was also a woman of interest in a murder case. As he started the ignition, his mind replayed the conversation and Kimberly's careful words. He knew he had to come back for another talk, but for now, he headed back to the station.
