In the picturesque world of paragliding, hidden secrets tumble as Detective Winston investigates the brutal hatchet murder of Travis, with only Bryan and Everett in the center of the storm.

Rubbing the backside of his eyes, Winston slowly navigated the case photos scattered across his desk. A paragliding site, bloody and as wide open as the sea, was the setting for Travis's murder. Bryan, known more for his cooking than as a suspect, stepped into the limelight of Winston's investigation. 

It did not go unnoticed that Bryan would carry a hatchet on him for his job; the tool in hand was a common sight that everyone had become accustomed to. Par for the course, it was largely ignored when Bryan was seen sharpening his utensil before the incident; a hatchet taught to kiss the air during Bryan's past hatchet throwing competitions. 

Travis was a known occurence on the local gliding scene. Bryan was his assistant, charged with food and drinks, presumably there to manage as the paragliders soared high above.

"So, you're always left to care for the gliders' needs during the flights, huh?" Winston asked, making sure to keep his tone casual as they approached Bryan, who was preparing a meal.

"Yeah, been doing it for a while now. Help 'em grab a bite at the end of their flight, you know?" Bryan mentioned, chopping some tough ingredients with his hatchet. From his posture and technique, it was clear he knew his way around such a tool.

"The same way you've been helping yourself to the petty cash, I see," Winston casually remarked, causing Bryan to stumble a bit, resulting in him nicking his finger slightly.

"No, that's not..." Bryan lapsed before continuing, his hands trembling. He seemed to be genuinely frightened of the possibility of going to jail.

"Travis didn't seem to think so," Winston subtly pointed out, before changing the topic. "How'd you feel about his pranks?"

Bryan's grip on his hatchet tightened, "He's... been a real handful. Those weren’t just pranks, he's been doing everything in his power to make a fool out of me."

"I suppose you were near the gliding site before the incident happened?" Bryan nodded, confirming that he indeed was, "Yeah, I was there prepping up the food and drinks we're serving today."

In the pink-tinged evening light, Winston walked back from the crime scene towards his car. Whispers of unfriendly pranks, public humiliation, and petty thefts filled the air. Across his mind slipped an image of Travis, alone, soaring in the air.

Detective Winston sat back in his chair, brows furrowed as he perused the pile of evidence on the sturdy wooden table. He meticulously studied the hapless victim - Travis, a man recently celebrated for his acrobatic skills on a paraglider, a man whose life was cut short at a paragliding site with a hatchet.

His suspect was intriguing, to say the least. Everett he was known as, a bright-faced man whose talent lay in the realm of woodworking methods. Interestingly, a majority of his time was dedicated to curating displays of impeccable craftsmanship at the local woodworking museum.

Upon arriving at the museum, Winston took a mental note of the serene aura surrounding Everett. His hands, worn from years of delicate crafting, fondly caressed the various tools in his personal collection. Quiet admiration sparked in his eyes as he studied each piece. The hatchet, which was the murder weapon, had been sourced from this same collection.

Everett had a dubious past, considering he had been privy to the office that housed a drawer filled with FFID cards, each bearing a different alias. The coincidental catalog of names was a matching list to Everett's known aliases.

In a room full of bustling conference attendees, Fraser, a local woodworker, casually recollected an incident about an 'Edward' who introduced himself during a conversation at a conference. This character sketch fit Everett impeccably. Yet another time, Winston learned, Everett introduced himself as 'Eric' within a gathering of familiar faces.

His evenly-toned voice was lit with envy as he recalled the numerous paragliding events where he would always find himself under the grand shadow of the deceased Travis. This bitterness was further accentuated by a recent event where Travis triumphed over Everett for a highly acclaimed paragliding award.

"Do you do much woodworking yourself?" Winston asked.

Everett's eyes softened, his hands gripped tighter around the intricate carving in his hand. "Yes, indeed," he replied. "It's the one thing that brings me peace..."

Parallel to the photo of Travis, paragliding expert propelled to international fame, an unsigned artisan found solace in chipping away at blocks of wood, longing for the same acclaim.

In the chilling depths of the swamp, Ricky was found silenced forever by a bottle of bleach, leaving Detective Winston the daunting task of deciphering the lethal motives of the prime suspects, Glenn and Tessa.

For Detective Winston, a seasoned investigator who had seen every shade of human nature, the affair of Ricky's murder seemed unusual. He detested the musky smell of the swamps where Ricky's body was found that same day. But of course, the repugnance a crime scene induces is not a criterion to be considered in investigations. 

His letters of introduction remarked that he would be received by Glenn, a local dentist. As Winston rounded upon the dental clinic, he couldn't fail to notice the tell-tale smell of sterilizing bleach that hung heavily in the air.

"Morning Doctor," Winston said as he walked into the clinic.

"Good Morning, How can I help you?" replied Glenn.

"My name is Winston. I am investigating the death of one Ricky," he explained.

Glenn visibly shuttered at the mention of Ricky's name, "I had seen him recently for a root canal."

Winston wasn't too surprised by this. Many victims' last known location turned out to be places where they had felt safe. He made a mental note of it but didn't engage in any further discussion about Ricky.

He noticed a desktop computer nearby where a dental science forum was open. Topics on toxicology and possible risk factors danced on the screen. "Is that what you were doing before I walked in?" Winston mused aloud.

"I was catching up on some forensic odontology discussions. It's my area of specialty," Glenn explained, sounding unusually enthusiastic about the subject. 

Tickets to Ricky's funeral were spread out on Glenn's desk, indicating that he'd likely be offering his last respects to the deceased individually. The dentist, a loner by appearance, never invites anyone to his remote house where he lives all by himself. This he didn't strike Winston as the kind to mingle at a social gathering.

Winston inquired about Glenn's whereabouts for most of the day Ricky was murdered, to which Glenn quickly responded, "I was out birdwatching at the swamp."

"But I heard you live in that isolated homestead," Winston said, diverting the conversation towards Glenn's personal life, "You don't usually invite anyone over?"

This time, Glenn didn't just show discomfort. He stammered and went pale. Clearly, his anxiety was rising at each personal question, 
and in an effort to divert the conversation, he interjected, "Do you know that prolonged use of teeth whitening treatment can cause oral cancer?" Winston was taken by surprise at the sudden change in conversation but chose not to question it any further. 

With that, his introduction to Glenn was over and his investigation continued.

Detective Winston pulled up to the prison, parking his car between the tall, barbed wire fences. Beyond them, he could see a swamp, the murky water shimmering with heat. Footsteps echoed through the sterile, concrete halls as he made his way inside, passing groups of colorfully uniformed prisoners on their way to and from various responsibilities. 

Brushing off some of the dust still clinging onto her orange jumpsuit, Tessa sat in the visiting room, the corners of her mouth curled into a hint of a smile. 

"Tessa," Winston began, "You work here on farms, correct?"

She nodded, crossing her arms over her chest, "Yeah, that's correct. We've got a swamp nearby too."

Winston wrote something down, answering with a nonchalant "Mmhhm."

"And before prison... you were a high school chemistry teacher, weren't you?"

"Yeah,” she grumbled, “From Bunsen burners to mop buckets."

"So, your current job here... cleaning, right?" to which Tessa confirmed. 

"And in turn, they provide you the cleaning supplies?"

"Yep,” she mused, “A mop, bucket, soap, gloves... bleach. Everything a good custodian ought to need." 

Winston scooted himself forward a bit, "You were disciplined once for using bleach incorrectly, right?"

Her face turned expressionless. "That was years ago. Nothing but some harmless experiments." Tessa asserted.

As minutes rolled into hours, the conversation moved onto the victim, Ricky. Ruffling in his seat, Winston asked about the dwindling debt between Tessa and Ricky. 

"He couldn't just wait, huh? Always pestering about the damn debt. I tried to repay him, but it just never seemed enough." Tessa confessed, clenching her fist, "He even threatened me over it."

Underneath the fluorescent lights, Winston could see her distress - unable to keep up with Ricky's demands despite her financial limitations. 

Remembering his autopsy briefing, Winston knew Ricky was found in the very swamp near the prison's farm. Perhaps, Tessa knew something...

"Ricky's body was found near the swamp, past the farm." Winston stated.

A flicker of shock passed through Tessa's eyes before her face returned back to its hardened, impassive state. She may not have expected anyone would find him, or for the news to reach her this quickly. "Near the farm, within the walking distance he murmured..."

He thanked her for talking and left, leaving Tessa alone in the visiting room. 

As he walked back through the dense crowd of prisoners, past the pungent smell of bleach cleaning the hallways, Winston realized, this was going to be a difficult case to crack. A life lost over a debt, and the swamp held many secrets yet to reveal.

In the dimly lit corners of a rundown motel, Jimmy's life was abruptly silenced by the ominous echo of a revolver, leaving Detective Winston with two enigmatic suspects - Isla, with her elusive charm, and Randy, the taciturn stranger.

Winston sat in the dimly lit diner across from Randy, who was picking at his meal. Randy was a tall, thin man with a head of unruly hair, loosely holding onto a crushed, rather worn looking guitar pick. Seemed like a regular musician, but Winston knew that eyes can deceive. He started the conversation, coaxing out bits and pieces of Randy's most recent trials. 

"Rumor has it you're having some trouble paying off loans, Randy," Winston ventured. 

The musician looked up from his plate, setting his fork down. "Yeah, you heard right," Randy confessed. 

Winston waited a beat, then asked, "Got any other vices we should know about?"

Randy chuckled grimly. "Well, I have a knack for getting my money into the wrong hands at the poker table."

Winston nodded, making a note of it. Before moving onto the next subject, he specified, "Got news yesterday - a revolver was found, identical to the one you were seen with at a music concert. It turned out to be the murder weapon." 

Randy paused and shrugged. "Got it for protection. You never know who you might run into on the road. I only ever use it for shooting at the range."

Whilst Randy was talking, Winston noticed the deep scars on Randy's fingers in the dim neon light. They were all identical in their presence, all etched with the same depth and characteristics. Being a man of detail, Winston asked Randy about them.

"Those?" Randy looked at his hands with a sad laughter. "Each scar on my hand came from a different guitar string breaking at a concert, all of them had a unique tale to tell," he said. Then he added, "usual guitar injuries are just mere blisters, not deep scars like these. But what can I say? Bad luck follows me around".

Winston, though intrigued, refrained from reading anything into it. He then moved the conversation toward Randy's past interactions with the victim, the international hotel mogul, Jimmy.

“So you knew Jimmy. The guy owned hotels from Tokyo to New York,” Winston stated.

"Jimmy, he loved his opulence. Always surrounded by luxury," Randy shrugged. "Not that I ever got a slice of it, of course. I played in a few of his hotels... never got the invite to the penthouse." 

Winston thanked Randy for his time and left the diner. There were more aspects of this case to sniff out. All in a day’s work.

Detective Winston sat across from Isla at the local coffee shop, the smell of burnt coffee wafting around them. 

Isla played less of a nervous suspect and leaned more into her usual friendly demeanor. Although they usually ran into each other at the gym, today's meetup was not about catching up on fitness routines. Just the other day, she had confessed to a friend on the treadmill beside her that she couldn't bear the blackmail from Jimmy anymore.

"Jimmy...he...he was blackmailing me, Detective Winston," Isla confessed, bleakly stirring her coffee. Her hopelessness was clear, something she had mentioned to her friends recently regarding the relentless blackmail. 

Winston didn't show his surprise. He just nodded and gestured for her to continue. 

"We used to meet at a motel down the road. Crazy, right? But it was the only place we could talk without being seen. I was even there on the day of the murder," Isla confessed. That fact was uncovered in a police report which witnessed Isla at the motel on the day of Jimmy's murder.

Winston knew this already, having received a report of Isla being spotted with Jimmy at the motel quite a few times in the past. He just grunted, encouraging her to keep speaking. 

"It's not what you think. He...he took some photos...and threatened to expose them." Isla shuddered, her coffee cup rattling in her hand. 

"Did you ever confront him about it?" Winston asked, looking unwaveringly at Isla. 

"Yes, I did! I couldn't stand it any longer, Detective. That day...the day he was killed...I was going to tell him it had to stop," Isla admitted, her voice raw with emotion. 

"And then what happened?" Winston asked, watching Isla's face carefully. 

"I...I don't remember," Isla said, running a hand through her hair. "I was so worked up. I just...I ended up at the shooting range. It helps...calm me down."

Winston groaned internally on hearing this. Isla had been seen at the shooting range more often than not lately, supposedly to "blow off some steam". On one occasion, she had talked extensively about her growing gun collection to another gym buddy, which was a recurring topic she loved to discuss with anyone who'd lend an ear. She was often heard discussing different types of firearms amidst these conversations. 

"Do you remember what time it was when you left the range?" Winston asked. But Isla shook her head, looking gloomy, and didn't say a word. 

Winston sighed and checked his watch. The interview was close to being over, and he needed to gather more facts to help solve the case. But in the back of his mind, he couldn't help but dwell on the circumstances... Hopeless. Desperate. A lineup of damning coincidences. But the one most nagging thought that lingered as he got up to leave was the overpowering scent of burnt coffee: just how much it reminded him of gunpowder.

Target case file:

In the tranquil solitude of a secluded chalet, Clyde meets an untimely death from snake venom; a case which sees the sharp mind of Detective Winston matching wits with two elusive suspects, Mack and Taylor.

As Winston walked into the sleek design studio, everything looked like it was out of a luxurious catalog. Mack, the man responsible for the rich interior designs was engrossed in sketching a new collection, his exotic reptile sculptures reflecting his extensive knowledge of reptile anatomy and he was known for keeping up with the latest snake discoveries as part of his hobby. 

“You Mack?” Winston asked, catching the man's attention. Mack turned to face the detective, revealing a chiseled face accentuated with some disturbing scars. 

"Mack's who you're chattin' to now." His tone was casual but assertive. His posture was confident, but his eyes, they held a disconcerting intensity, like a reptile about to strike. 

Winston was about to ask about the intriguing designs, instead, Mack strode across the room to a glass terrarium. He sifted his way through a mess of receipts on the barren desk to pull out a small, clear plastic box. 

"I've a hobby that keeps me distracted from work sometimes. Reptiles... snakes, to be precise. A passion I picked up in college," he said. He chuckled a little as he offered some snake food to the terrifying critter, its vibrant colors making one's blood run cold.

On noticing the detective's curiosity regarding the terrarium and the snake held within, Mack revealed, "Ah, she's a recent purchase. A gorgeous specimen of venomous elegance," a peculiar gleam in Mack's eyes as he stared back at the snake, locked in an uncanny understanding.

Winston's gaze wandered to the vast array of receipts adorning the studio desk, most of them marked for snake food and terrarium equipment. But nothing here attached the man to the scars on his face. Curiosity piqued he attempted to steer the conversation towards the scars.

However, Mack's expression immediately hardened, curtly shifting the conversation to something less personal, "That's not your concern, detective." It was evident then; Mack wasn’t one to let others take control of the conversation. 

As the detective prepared to leave, Mack added, “I don't get out much. A lot of work crammed here, keeps me pinned down." His eyes darted towards a letter, one discovered amongst a pile of threatening letters. All unmistakably written in Clyde’s handwriting rightly threatening Mack’s sister. 

"Ever deal with Clyde?" Winston inquired. "I confronted him about his threats to my sister, and that's when Clyde audaciously admitted to them," Mack bravely confessed. He further added that he reported the assault immediately after it happened, one he unfortunately happened to witness.

Suitably intrigued, Winston respectfully excused himself with the promise of returning. He found Mack to be a complex subject, snakes, design, and all. The circumstances around Mack and his relation to Clyde evidently needed a more in-depth look.

Winston rubbed his aching temples as he scrutinized the information sprawled across his desk. It had been a long day, and the recent news of Clyde's death hadn't provided any form of convenience.

He fixated his attention on his prime suspect, Taylor, the adoptive mother of the victim. Her profession as a snake specialist had always struck him as odd, especially now, in a case involving snake venom. Winston slid the calendar invite across the table. “So, you had a day scheduled with Clyde at his chalet, the day of his... incident? A whole day alone with him according to this...”

Taylor nodded softly, her voice was barely above a whisper. "Just chance... We always planned mother-son days. He loved that chalet. We spent long periods alone there, just us. But things were different that day... I was... scared."

"In public, Clyde wasn't any easier either. There were numerous events where he would explode in anger, catching the sight of all those around him," Winston said, recalling the instances of Clyde's violent outbursts that he had documented from his surveys.

In the hours Winston spent with Taylor, he noted how she seemed on edge. Her eyes darted around the room, clothing neatly arranged, concealing what he suspected might be the aftermath of several violent confrontations. His suspicion was soon confirmed when he found a stack of hospital records tucked away at Taylor’s home detailing her prior injury treatments.

"Clyde... He got angry often, and I was always the target," Taylor admitted when Winston confronted her with the records. "He sometimes had violent outbursts in public too, but he was my son. I stayed. I always tried to stay safe. Most of my work is behind the glass. You know, handling snakes only under controlled circumstances. Some are venomous, yes."

"Was Clyde aware of the risks in dealing with venomous snakes?" Winston pressed on, folding his hands atop the table, leaning in, looking for answers within Taylor's eyes. 

"Of course," Taylor replied. "I've had to explain to him before... How the venom works. Why it's dangerous. Even how it's administered if mishandled... But the fear... Clyde was terrifying."

Through her narrative, Winston realized how comfortable she was around venomous snakes, a fact that only heightened his suspicion. He always found such risky professions unnerving.  

Further interviews with Clyde's friends confirmed Taylor's account of his violent tendencies. In fact, Clyde had confided his plans of spending the day with his mother at the chalet only to these friends. Other than Taylor, nobody else was seen at the chalet during the time of the incident. 

Inspecting all the data, Winston realized he'd woven together a vast yet mystifying narrative. He reassured Taylor one final time before exiting. "Thank you Taylor, I will be in touch."

As he left Taylor's abode, he took one last glance at her. He noticed the fear in her eyes, and he knew, her trauma was far from over.

context:
Background files from related investigations (some may be irrelevant):

In the unforgiving desert landscape, Philip's lifeless body was discovered, a nunchaku the ghastly cause of his demise, leaving Detective Winston on a barren hunt, with Jim and Woodrow as his prime suspects.

Winston was stationed in his dusty sedan, parked down the street from a local second-hand shop. The thrift shop had a distinctive sign above its doorway "Woodrow's Antiques & Collectibles". 

His destination was not the thrift store though but the old man sitting in the wooden rocking chair on the front porch of the house just behind the store. 

Squaring his shoulders, Winston exited his car and approached the man. The old man nodded at his approach. "Mister Woodrow?" Winston asked. 

"That I am. And you don't look like a fan of knick-knacks. So I presume you're a detective?"

"Guilty as charged," Winston replied with a light chuckle. "Mind if I ask you a few questions?" 

"It's my property, detective. Love the solitude out here. I usually enjoy my peace but, go ahead," Woodrow motioned toward an empty chair opposite him. Winston noticed the hard lines of Woodrow’s arms, the strong muscles present even in his old age. 

Winston opened his notebook, "So, you used to teach martial arts?"

Woodrow smiled, "Yes, indeed. For about 40 years. Even collected a few martial arts pieces during my teaching days. Nunchaku among others," he said pointing towards a small wooden room, laden with antiques and relics.

"You still practice?"

"Everyday," Woodrow responded. "Keeps me young."

Winston checked his notes reminiscing, "The police called me after Philip mentioned he was invited here to your desert property. You had a visit from him recently, didn't you?"

Woodrow stiffened at the name. "Yeah, we got together here at my desert property."

Winston lean forward, "Philip... his actions towards the family, they were consistently abusive, weren't they?"

Woodrow sighed heavily, "Yes, that's true. Bad blood doesn't spoil the family, detective. Philip... he made many mistakes, constantly crossing lines. He never even showed an ounce of remorse. It's been difficult, but I love my family dearly and I do everything in my power to protect them," Woodrow explained, a hint of pain in his aged eyes.

Winston nodded, jotting down notes, "Did Philip come alone on his visit?"

"Yeah," Woodrow confirmed. "Needed help with his car, he said. Practically humiliated me in public when it went down. But yeah... he came, and I was here. Alone."

"Well, thank you for your time, Woodrow," Winston closed his notebook, standing up. 

"Don't mention it, detective," Woodrow replied, attention already diverted to his karate dummy in the corner of his sizeable yard.

Winston gave Woodrow one last glance and then set off back to his car, leaving Woodrow alone to his solitude. As he pulled away, he glanced in his rearview mirror to see Woodrow had already begun his martial arts practice for the day.

Winston squinted as the sun reflected off the desert's sands, making the sandy terrain that much hotter. As someone familiar with this environment, Jim often frequented the desert for solitude. Winston was investigating the intriguing murder of Philip and was heading to meet up with Jim, a local dockworker and a person of interest along with his co-workers, Joe and Sam.

Upon reaching Jim's dwelling in this arid scape, he noticed an interesting thing; despite living near the dock, Jim had a relatively dry, rougher demeanor, more suited to the desert heat. It was as if he often retreated to the desert for solitude. Joining him were Joe and Sam, each with their own questions to ask.

Joe casually started the conversation, asking Jim about his likes and dislikes. "Any hobbies you particularly enjoy, Jim?"  Jim chose to talk about the latest football match, his eyes oddly detached despite the commentary. Jim was often evasive when speaking about himself. "What about your family, Jim?", Joe continued. Jim responded, as he often does, with "I'd rather not talk about it."

During their coffee break, Sam tried to steer their conversation towards a lighter topic. "Jim," he asked, "what's your favourite film?" Jim masterfully deflected, changing the subject, commenting about the how the weather reminded him of days when he found solitude in the desert. Noticing this, Sam attempted again, asking Jim about his family, only to receive the same brief, vague answer that always followed inquiries about his private life. "I'd rather not talk about it," was Jim's curt response.

Meanwhile, Winston slowly pushed on his investigation. "Where were you on the night of 15th?", Winston asked gently, securing Jim’s response, "Night of the 15th, officer? Well, I had no work scheduled that day." His accent was thick and laced with something Winston couldn't put his finger on.

Probing gently, Winston asked. "What were you doing in the desert then?" Jim curtly responded, as he often did when being questioned, with "I'd rather not talk about it." His walls visibly starting to come up. A few witnesses had even claimed seeing Jim in the desert often in solitude.

Raising the tension, Winston brought up the topic of the document Philip had discovered concerning Jim's illegal operation at the docks, while also gently highlighting that Jim owed Philip a significant debt. Jim finally admitted to being alone with Philip that day in the desert, which he frequented, who had come to confront him about the debt.

On Philip's murder that happened in the desert while he was in solitude, Jim didn't say much, only admitting to being present in the desert that day. Unphased, Winston mentioned how the ledger detailing illegal activities was found with Philip's corpse, briefly catching a flicker of panic on Jim's face.

Returning to his evasive manner, Jim, when asked about the ledger replied with his typical refrain, "I'd rather not talk about it.", only heightening Winston's suspicions. Revelled in the tension of the meeting, Winston picked up his hat, wiped off the sweat, and left Jim with his thoughts, contemplating his next steps in this twisted desert murder. Meanwhile, the unanswered questions proposed by Joe and Sam added an extra layer of mystery to be unraveled.

In the winding passages of a labyrinth, Lauren meets her untimely death by nail gun, pulling Detective Winston into a complex maze of lies and danger where Rose and Aubrey become his primary suspects.


Winston sat in his dimly lit office, peering over the case details. The name Lauren frequented his mind as he evaluated the circumstances of her death. It was a unique scene to say the least, a murder inside a labyrinth, with a nail gun as the murder weapon of choice.

His focus then diverted to the name that was on everyone's lips: Rose. She was Lauren's stepsister and her profession stood out to him the most. Rose was a carpenter; she was often required to read blueprints for her job, and had comprehensive knowledge about nail guns due to her regular use of them at work. As it happened, the blueprint of the labyrinth where the body was found was posted at her jobsite. An interesting coincidence, Winston thought, but he knew better than to jump to conclusions.

Rose's gang involvement made matters more complicated. As a member of a local gang that took their reputation seriously, she found herself enmeshed in scenarios where respect was the ultimate currency. Winston remembered hearing about a notorious gathering of the gang where Lauren had called Rose a loser. To publicly humiliate her in front of her fellow gang members like that had not been taken lightly. What bothered Winston was that despite Rose being present at a community event nearby, no one noticed her in the labyrinth that day.

Conviction settled within Winston. He needed to talk to Rose. Grabbing his coat, he exited the office, his mind reflecting the image of the carpenter, wrapped in the complexities of Lauren's murder. Little did he know, the clues were only beginning to unfold.

Detective Winston put away the photos of the crime scene he was investigating. The labyrinth where Lauren was found, held a certain eerie mystique to it. He began by interviewing the suspect, Aubrey.

Walking into the office of Aubrey was like walking into a different time period. The room was grand and ornate, filled with all types of frames and decor, managed by none other than Aubrey himself, the boss of the esteemed business.

Winston started the conversation careful not to rush. "You designed the labyrinth?" he asked, nodding.

A look of pride crossed Aubrey's face, "Yes, indeed. I even supervised its construction."

Winston casually inquired, "And the labyrinth is part of the business property, I presume?"

"Most definitely. It's a showcase, so to speak," Aubrey said.

Winston continued the conversation but his attention was drawn by a box in a display case on Aubrey's desk. The box was labeled "Keepsake". "What's in the box?" he asked.

Aubrey looked slightly taken aback before he smiled, "Oh, that. It's a lock of hair from someone who owed me. This person owed me and this is my keepsake," he admitted with an air of nonchalance.

A brief silence followed. Breaking it, Winston continued, "The labyrinth. Pretty difficult to navigate, I assume. Any blueprints or maps for it?"

Aubrey half shook his head, "The labyrinth is an enigma, detective, designed to challenge and confound. There are no public maps or blueprints for it."

Winston couldn't help but notice a defaced picture in Aubrey's collection. It was a photo of a once close friend, the eyes had been scratched out thoroughly. "What happened to the picture?" Winston asked. 

Aubrey didn't take a second to respond, "A moment of rage. I was angry at betrayal by an old friend. I scratched the eyes out and after the argument, I put it back in there." 

Later on, Winston found out about a whispered overheard conversation Aubrey had about Lauren's betrayal as Aubrey was outside Lauren's house. Apparently, Aubrey had overheard a conversation between Lauren and a competitor. This lead to the argument and defacement of the photo.

After the conversation with Aubrey, Winston got a hint towards Aubrey's character. Before he left, Winston asked, "You have access to that labyrinth, correct?"

"Of course," confirmed Aubrey, "I have master keys to all parts of my property."

It was after Winston visited Lauren's residence that he found copies of confidential business documents clearly indicating her plans of betrayal. Lauren had planned to sell secrets to a known rival. 

"This case," muttered Winston, "is starting to look like a veritable labyrinth itself."

Target case file:

In the heart of bustling Times Square, Johnny's life was abruptly ended with an unlikely weapon—a trident—and now, Detective Winston must unravel the murky truths hidden behind suspects Jay and Karl.

Winston peered at the case file and twitched his cigarette. Another one bit the dust in Times Square, a pretty common sight as of late. Jay, the regular local of the square, had made another one of his notorious catches, or so he seemed to be trying to. This time, however, it wasn't in the joy of celebration. 

Arresting the immediate crime scene routine, it came to an adoptive father. Jay, a man who loved his adopted son, Johnny, as deeply as his own blood. Unmistakably, he treated him with undying affection. Jay was a local fisherman, known to bait his lines and toss his nets in Times Square us with unusual regularity.

Winston was no stranger to the peculiar. A man making his catch amidst the solemn sea of humanity seemed alien yet plausible in ways nothing else could be. Winston lit another cigarette, his eyes tracing the hotel reservation confirmation in Jay’s name at a nearby hotel; Jay was also at Times Square for New Year's celebrations.

Now, that wasn’t unusual. After all, many locals booked rooms not far to be around the electric New Year’s celebration. Johnny, too, was part of the cacophony that night, showering in the confetti rain and the bursts of fireworks.

A cold shiver ran down Winston's spine as he recalled a conversation he had picked up where Jay overheard Johnny's intention to expose his illegal fishery.

The dynamics between a father and son duo is a complex bond. Johnny had officially registered himself under Jay’s guardianship quite a while ago, and now his disclosure had ignited an unexpected storm. 

Winston dropped his gaze onto the pictures of Jay's house. A noticeable collection caught his eyes. A vast array of tridents, carefully displayed and proudly shown off to any guest entering his abode. With an uneasiness settling over him, Winston noted that one of the tridents was strikingly similar to the weapon linked to Johnny's murder.

Winston took the last puff of his cigarette, and he ground the stub into the ashtray, turning over all the facts in his head. Already, the investigation looked murky, muddled with familial ties and sinister events.

Despite the rising sun casting long shadows, the path before Winston remained dark.

It was time to interview Jay, Winston decided, as he pieced together the intricate pattern connecting paternity, fishing, and a bloody murder.

Winston viewed the stark crime scene photos of Johnny's brutal murder in Times Square. The murder weapon was a trident, an oddity in any case, which only added to the eerie nature of Times Square, a place that seemed to attract all sorts of outlandish incidents.

His only solid lead so far was stock broker Karl, whom Johnny had been suspicious of. Karl was known to deal with more than just Wall Street, handling the financial investments of some of the most prominent celebrities. Well-known for his connections and unconventional tactics, it was rumored that he often used insider information for personal gain, a decidedly illegal maneuver on the stock market.

During their final showdown, Johnny had threatened to go to the police with evidence that pointed to Karl's crooked stock manipulations. But Johnny was brutally murdered before he could even do so. Now, as he viewed the images of Johnny's murder, Winston felt a deepening sense of dread.

It was time to question Karl. Upon arrival in the heart of Wall Street where Karl had his office, he found a bustling hub of blue suits. Amidst this flurry, Karl stood out, impeccably dressed and complete with a cordial smile he typically saved for his high-profile clients.

"Greetings, Detective," Karl said calmly.

"Good afternoon, Karl," Winston replied, keeping his tone neutral. "Can we have a moment to speak in private?"

In Karl's luxurious private office, an array of historical weapons adorned the walls, an unusual decorative taste for a corporate figure. Winston began the conversation stating the facts he already knew, "So you're a fan of historical weapons?"

"Not just a fan," Karl replied, putting on a proud smile, "Last summer, I even took lessons in trident fighting. It's all part of my personal life that I’d rather keep to myself. I’m not too fond of sharing personal information."

Upon digging deeper into Karl's dealings, Karl became visibly uncomfortable. His stiff body language indicated that he wasn't too keen on discussing his personal life further. Winston, however, continued to press on, bringing up Johnny and the documents he had left behind before his death - evidence of Karl's illegal stock manipulation.

Karl retained an impressively unflappable demeanor, revealing no hints of guilt or remorse. However, the mention of Johnny and the documents seemed to create a ripple in his stoic shell.

Then a call came to Winston's phone; it was his assistant informing him of the result of the search at Karl's house. Among the collection of historical artifacts and weapons, a trident was found - a chilling answer to the choice of murder weapon.

Confronting Karl with this latest discovery, Winston noticed a visible strain on Karl's face, his corporate mask slipping momentarily. After bidding him goodbye, Winston left the office, leaving a now silent Karl amongst his historical weapons and luxurious comforts. His passion for historical warfare had now become the primary focus of the murder investigation.
question: Who is the most likely murderer?

context:
Background files from related investigations (some may be irrelevant):

In the cold echo of a deserted hockey rink, Otis was found dead from a grenade explosion, and now Detective Winston must decipher the clues, suspecting Ervin and Andrew are somehow involved.

Detective Winston rubbed his temples while the facts flickered across his computer screen. Otis, the victim, would most definitely be missed. His usual vibrant energy that filled the hockey rink was replaced by cold, solemn silence.

Some contradictions needed to be resolved. The crime scene at the hockey rink was empty, both at the time of the murder and throughout the investigation. Winston's only lead was Andrew, who was an old military pal of Otis. Winston heard that Andrew had recently switched his career to become a solo hiking guide. Indeed, a remarkable part of his solo hikes was his ability to help hikers they came across on the way overcome environmental dangers—a way of applying his skills acquired from his military service. It was an unusual practice in the industry but allowed due to his military expertise in bomb disposal—an odd career choice for a man of such skills.

Winston drove to the outskirts of the town, where Andrew lived in a remote cabin. Andrew's solo job didn't always welcome company, but that didn't seem to bother him. Rumor had it that he uses his military skills to help strangers on the trails overcome environmental dangers—detonating falling rocks, perhaps?

Once in the cabin, Winston noticed several hiking supplies meticulously arranged. He inspected them and found, hidden strategically among the normal hiking necessities—food, water, emergency kit—were several small explosives. Chills ran down his spine as he remembered a recent break-in at a military base.

"I see you have explosives mixed with your hiking guide supplies,” Winston said, trying to evoke a reaction.

Andrew replied calmly, “Those are just for emergencies.”

Listening to Andrew, Winston remembered that Otis had been friendly with him. Otis was always open with Andrew about his daily habits, even shared his calendar with him. Andrew was the only person who knew Otis would be alone at the hockey rink that evening.

On his way out, Winston remembered Andrew's frank words, "I don't like to hang out after work.”

It seemed somewhat true, living far from town, working alone, and being prone to avoid after-work hangouts. Winston thought to himself: Andrew did like to be alone. It all seemed so strange, the grenade murder, the empty hockey rink, Andrew’s distant demeanor. However, he couldn't draw any obvious conclusions just yet. He needed more.

Detective Winston sat on the chilly bleachers of the local hockey rink, a place as familiar to him as it was to Ervin, the mild-mannered Rabbi who had never missed a game. The rink was still splattered with telltale signs of the merciless violence that had taken place there. Otis had been killed during a game, a seemingly jovial event turned nightmarish by the unexpected detonation of a grenade.

Taking his eyes off the crime scene momentarily, he scanned his surroundings and spotted his next person of interest: Ervin, a massive hockey fan, and a staunch supporter of their local team. His presence at the game had been expected, as his dedicated attendance was part of the everyday routine. Some of the spectators had mentioned Ervin stepping out of the stadium briefly, interestingly around the same time Otis was killed.

Not missing his beat, Winston approached Rabbi Ervin, who was still in deep shock at the loss of a fellow spectator and friend, “Rabbi Ervin?”

The Rabbi looked up to meet the detective's prying eyes, “I am Ervin, indeed. And you are?”

“I am Detective Winston, investigating the recent unfortunate event.”

Observing Ervin's face closely, Winston began: "The strangest thing happened a few days ago. Otis came to me and told me he was planning to go to the authorities. He knew something was off, dangerous even. I guess we didn't react quickly enough. He mentioned your name, Ervin, and something about another life before the synagogue…”

Ervin was quiet, his gaze distant but thoughtful. "Yes, Otis did confront me. He saw me moving some funds around. He saw, Detective, he saw me committing the crime which I've regretted every day since," Ervin confessed.

Winston let the confession sink in before shifting the subject subtly. "I heard you were in the military?"

Ervin smiled, just barely, nodding with a touch of pride. "Yes, I am a former military officer. Had a special training in demolitions you see, before I found my calling in religion."

Winston returned his smile, "I suppose it's a bit of a leap from demolitions to the pulpit."

"Just a tad," Ervin's laughter is soft. "But the old life stays with you in ways you wouldn't expect. I've got a collection of war memorabilia back home. host some of my friends over sometimes, they marvel at these artifacts. I even got grenades in there. Nothing active, of course. They tend to catch the eye.”

Winston excused himself, leaving Ervin to mourn at the crash of their sanctuary of play turned battleground.

In the quiet of a home office, Mackenzie met a fiery end via a flamethrower, leaving Detective Winston tasked with questioning the two unlikely suspects, Sophia and Virgil.

Winston eyed the offensively ostentatious Ferrari parked in front of Virgil's house as he walked up the driveway. Virgil himself was standing in the front yard, admiring his Adonis-like physique in the car's reflective paint. His obscenely large biceps rippled as he flexed, each one larger than Winston's head. 

"Winston, Detective Winston. Can we talk?" Winston called out, causing Virgil to jump and spin around. Upon seeing Winston, a man of authority, Virgil noticeably tensed. His nostrils flaring, Virgil responded, "Alright, Detective. What's this about?" 

Winston watched as his gaze flicked back to the Ferrari and began, "I believe you know Mackenzie? You were seen at her house the day she was killed." Virgil's eyes widened a fraction but he quickly composed himself. He admitted, "Yes, I was there. She often asks me to move around some of her heavy furniture in her home office." 

"I heard a rumor Mackenzie mocked your achievement in bodybuilding and eventually sold your trophy," Winston added. Virgil bristled at the mention of Mackenzie's name, a flicker of something passing over his face. 

"Let's talk inside, feel more comfortable," Virgil said, leading Winston into his house. Virgil's house was immaculate. There was a separate room full of neatly categorized shelves crammed with documentaries and notebooks tagged with the names of the documentaries. The notebooks contained detailed diagrams, timelines and highlights of key events in the documentaries. It confirmed Winston's previous report that Virgil was quite into the True Crime genre. 

The most surprising feature in his house was a giant glass case, empty and dust-free. It was obviously a place for something too valued to be manhandled. "That empty spot used to be occupied by my bodybuilding trophy, an achievement that required countless hours in the gym and disciplined nutrition," Virgil said with a hard edge to his voice, "then Mackenzie took it, belittled my effort and sold it."

Winston's gaze flickered between the muscular man and the empty cabinet briefly before responding, "A champion bodybuilder, impressive. I heard about your hardship and dedication. Shame about the trophy, though, they're hard to replace." Virgil's eyes blazed with something akin to anger but he made no comment.

As he was leaving, Winston briefly considered the muscle-bound man. Witnesses who had seen him at Mackenzie's house on the day of the incident... his collection of true crime documentaries... Mackenzie's mockery and theft of his prized bodybuilding trophy. The facts were like an incomplete jigsaw puzzle. 

A thick layer of fear hung in the cool evening air as Winston headed back to his nondescript sedan.  The connections were apparent, but the answers weren’t. And he still had a long night ahead.

In the secluded quiet of his office, Winston nursed his scotch as he pored over the case file for Sophia, the prolific art collector. His investigation took a deep dive into the CCTV footage from the home of Mackenzie, Sophia's benefactor. As he studied the video, he noticed Sophia, a recurring figure, found on the grainy footage both at the foot of a local dealer’s four-story warehouse and Mackenzie's home, the same dealer who supplied Mackenzie's esteemed art collection.

“I’ve seen her around,” said Mackenzie’s neighbor on the shaky video clip, which Winston obtained from the CCTV mounted on Mackenzie's front porch. “She was here, at Mackenzie’s house. She comes by now and then to show off her new art pieces.”

During his late-night surveillance, Winston had footage of Sophia transporting flamethrowers into her art studio, an arresting sight, but less so when considering her chosen artistic medium. As dawn broke over the city, Winston observed Sophia's art studio, pinpointing comings and goings. Indeed, Sophia was handling a flamethrower, a tool he learned was frequently featured in her work. Her signature piece was a charred wooden structure, only achievable through the extensive use of a flamethrower.

Contacting Mackenzie, Winston discovered her involvement in Sophia's struggle with substances. Mackenzie confessed to finding Sophia's hidden stash inside her own house during a visit from Sophia. This shocking revelation precipitated her intervention. Mackenzie threatened to sever the financial lifeline she provided for Sophia's art unless Sophia sought recovery. In fact, Mackenzie warned of public disgrace if Sophia didn't get help, wanting the world to know of her addiction unless cured.

Inside Sophia's studio, Winston found sculptures that contained charred elements, hues possible only by the flame's lick. He also discovered stacks of unpaid bills, a barren bank account ledger, and tell-tale drug paraphernalia. This grim scene painted a clear picture of Sophia's financial desperation and her fiendish need for drugs. Not only was her art unique but also for sale. Mackenzie was interested in buying a certain piece - Sophia had agreed to this transaction, as evidenced by Mackenzie's name tacked on one of the art pieces.

Sophia's living arrangements reflected her financial ruin. A note from Mackenzie, garishly displayed on her wall, hinted at the ultimatum over art funds unless Sophia cleaned up her act, a common maneuver in attempts at addiction intervention.

In the sanctuary of Mackenzie's home office, Winston unearthed documents revealing Mackenzie's heavy financial involvement in Sophia's life. Her contributions extended to Sophia's seemingly exorbitant rent, endless supply of canvases, paint, and even the shadowy corners of her addiction - her drugs. Mackenzie was more to Sophia than just a client, she was her de facto financier, the backbone to her irresponsible indulgence.

With this newfound perspective of the complexities of Sophia's life, Winston discovered evidence of newly discovered drug stash tucked away in an unassuming plastic bag marked with Sophia’s initials, found in Mackenzie's office. Sophia’s tangled web of deception began to unravel, but Winston remained composed. His mission was to discover and present the facts, navigating through the labyrinthine maze of lies.

Target case file:

In the bustling mayhem of the city mall, a man falls fatally to the seldom-seen weapon of a sai; it's up to the cunning and relentless Detective Winston to interrogate his only leads, Peyton and Isolde.

Engrossed in his case files, Winston took a sip of his cold coffee. A quick brushing of the autopsy report led him to understand the brutal nature of Guy's death... by way of a Sai.

Upon inquiring further into the murder weapon, he found out about a certain niece, Peyton, who was identified as a collector of such items. Weapons, all different kinds, were Peyton's obsession. Her fixation was so strong that it even crossed over to her recreational time, she took martial arts classes weekly. 

A thought popped into Winston's mind and he felt a sudden rush of adrenaline; Peyton was also proficient with the sai. The words of her martial arts instructor echoed in his mind, "Peyton is proficient with the sai and many other weapons. She almost scared me with her skill."

Winston moved on to Peyton's employment status. She worked daytime shifts. Interesting, he thought, as the mall murder had taken place at night. A leak about Peyton shopping frequently at the murder scene and her evident fondness for shopping only seemed to deepen the investigation.

Recalling a statement of one of Guy's friends, he said, 'Guy told me he was planning to expose Peyton's secret'. Guy was about to spill Peyton's secret, and she had reacted to this threat fearfully, as if something precious was at stake. Winston remembered hearing the intense words Peyton had uttered "I won't let you ruin me, Guy!" Her secret was something she was desperate to keep hidden.

He crumpled the empty coffee cup in his hand. Time to speak to Peyton.
 
As he drove off, he couldn't help but wonder. Just what was Peyton's secret? And what lengths did she go to, to keep it hidden? Winston knew he had to tread lightly, every piece of the puzzle mattered, even more so when everyone was a suspect.

The constant clinking of glasses and din of jovial voices filled the air as Winston idled near the polished oak bar. His eyes were focused on the bartender - a stern-looking woman named Isolde. He had heard the rumors about her refusing service to customers from Guy's ethnic background, and those claims had piqued his interest. Guy himself had complained to his family about this, and the distaste in their voices as they spewed recounts of the tales was a clear indicator of the gravity of the situation. Isolde was not just known for her reputation as a martinet bartender but was also notable for her martial arts prowess, evident when she was seen practicing with sai at her martial arts school. Her frequent sai practice sessions at the school held his attention tonight.
 
Leaning on the edge of the bar, he made eye contact with her. Isolde's expression was guarded as she glanced at him once, appearing hesitant because of the past. Guy's coworkers, who frequented the very bar, had shared stories of hearing racial slurs she had thrown at Guy. They had also relayed these offensive exchanges to Guy's family, fueling the flame that Winston was now looking into. He recognized her from those recounts, the complaints about the woman named Isolde vivid in his memory.

Meeting her gaze, he gestured to the collection of martial arts DVDs displayed at one corner of the bar. "Into martial arts movies, I see."

Isolde’s eyes lit up momentarily, "Absolutely. Their craft, the plot twist…nothing beats it!" She was known to vouch for these movies, frequently recommending them to curious customers, as she did now with him. Her deep love for these films was quite apparent as she quoted lines from them frequently, the quotes seamlessly merging into her bar-side conversations.

Observing the martial arts weapons mounted on the walls behind the bar, Winston's eyes landed on a wall-mounted sai set. Distinctively, a vacant slot stood in the otherwise complete collection. During the investigation in her bar, a sai from the set was found missing. The rumor circulating was that the sai reported as Guy's murder weapon had eerily similar markings as the ones in Isolde's set.

"Nice collection," Winston said, pushing his empty glass forward "I will have another. Do you also train with these?"

"Always," Isolde responded while working on his drink, pride apparent in her voice. "I hold a pretty high rank at my martial arts school."

Moving on to less savory topics, Winston treaded cautiously. He mentioned seeing a few of her offensive posts on social media. Public posts that specialized in racial slander, foul comments directed towards members of Guy's race. Guy had told him about these posts, how they pained him to see such a blatant display of disrespect. They had all heard these derogatory comments, remembered her posting them on that unusually loud megaphone of hers - the internet.

Isolde noticeably stiffened but kept her silence, surely aware that these open refusals to serve customers, based on their ethnic backgrounds, had led to a flurry of complaints. Her behavior gave him pause, her hostility towards Guy perceived in her demeanor. Winston sighed, thinking about Guy and his coworkers, who had overheard the hostile conversations during their visits.

Winston finished his drink, neatly placing a folded cash note on the table. As he stood up to leave, a sly smile curled up on his lips. This, above everything else, was just the beginning. He exited quietly, leaving Isolde to mull over their conversation and the consequences that might ensue.
question: Who is the most likely murderer?
